note: Poetry Codex glossary of poetic terms. Definitions written by the editors; examples quoted from the archive's own texts (l: the lines as ?l= counts them).

terms.short: A four-line Greek lyric stanza named after Alcaeus, much used by Horace.
terms.long: Alcaeus of Lesbos (c. 600 BC) gave his name to this stanza of two long lines, a third of nine syllables and a fourth of ten, in a fixed pattern of long and short syllables. Horace made it the main stanza of his Odes. English poets (Tennyson's 'Milton', Clough's 'Alcaics') tried to reproduce it by stress. Its first two lines each have eleven syllables with a break after the fifth; the third and fourth differ, and the movement of the last two lines gives the stanza a characteristic swing. Imitating it in English, which hears stress rather than length, is a technical challenge that has attracted scholarly poets.

terms.short: A line of twelve syllables; in English, an iambic hexameter.
terms.long: The alexandrine is the great line of French classical verse (Racine, Corneille), named, it is said, after medieval French romances of Alexander the Great. In English it appears mostly as a single long line to close a stanza or vary couplets: the ninth line of the Spenserian stanza, or the occasional long line in Dryden. Pope mocked its misuse in An Essay on Criticism with an alexandrine that drags along as slowly as it says.

lines: A needless Alexandrine ends the song
That, like a wounded snake, drags its slow length along.
examples.title: An Essay on Criticism
examples.author: Alexander Pope
examples.why: Pope's demonstration: the second line is itself an alexandrine.

Fierce warres and faithfull loues shall moralize my song.
examples.title: The Faerie Queene · Book I, Canto I
examples.author: Edmund Spenser
examples.why: The second line here is the alexandrine that ends Spenser's first stanza.

terms.short: A story in which characters and events stand systematically for ideas or moral qualities.
terms.long: In allegory the literal narrative carries a second meaning throughout: the Redcrosse Knight is Holiness, his lady Una is Truth, the monster Error is error. Medieval and Renaissance literature loved it: the Romance of the Rose, Piers Plowman, Everyman, The Faerie Queene, The Pilgrim's Progress. Dream visions are often allegorical. Allegory differs from symbolism in that its meanings are usually systematic and sustained throughout the work, while symbols may be open and ambiguous. Readers of allegory are invited to interpret on more than one level at once: the literal story, the moral lesson and sometimes political or religious meanings.

examples.title: The Faerie Queene · Book I, Canto I
examples.author: Edmund Spenser
examples.why: Error, the first monster the Redcrosse Knight meets, half serpent and half woman.

terms.short: Repetition of the same initial consonant sound in nearby words.
terms.long: In Old English verse alliteration is the structural rule of the line; in later verse it is an ornament, used to bind phrases, imitate sounds or add emphasis. Hopkins, steeped in Welsh and Old English verse, made it a principle of his rhythm. Alliteration appeals to the ear, so it is especially strong in poetry meant to be heard, and it is common in proverbs, slogans and tongue-twisters. In English verse after the Middle Ages, it is usually decorative: a binding of key words, as in Shakespeare's 'from fairest creatures we desire increase'.

terms.short: The verse of Old English and Germanic poetry, in which each line has four stresses linked by alliteration across a central pause.
terms.long: Old English poetry does not rhyme or count syllables. Each line has two half-lines divided by a strong pause, each half with two main stresses, and the stressed syllables are bound by alliteration: the first stress of the second half-line (the 'head-stave') alliterates with one or both stresses of the first half. All vowels alliterate with one another. Beowulf, The Wanderer and The Seafarer are in this metre, and it returned in the fourteenth-century 'alliterative revival' of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and Piers Plowman. Gummere's Beowulf imitates it in modern English.

terms.short: A passing reference to another text, person or event, which the reader is expected to recognise.
terms.long: Allusion lets a poem draw on everything its reader knows. Milton's Paradise Lost alludes constantly to the Bible and the classics; Keats's sonnet on Chapman's Homer alludes to Cortez and the Pacific (in fact Balboa first saw it). Allusions can be learned or popular, solemn or ironic. An allusion is not a quotation: it can be a single word or name that brings a whole story with it. Allusions reward readers who recognise them, and part of the work of reading older poetry is to recover the shared knowledge that its first readers took for granted.

lines: Or like stout Cortez when with eagle eyes
He star'd at the Pacific--and all his men
examples.title: On First Looking into Chapman's Homer
examples.author: John Keats
examples.why: Keats's allusion to the Spanish conqueror's first sight of the Pacific.

terms.short: A metrical foot of two unstressed syllables followed by a stressed one: de-de-DUM.
terms.long: Anapaestic verse gallops. Byron's 'The Destruction of Sennacherib' uses it for an attacking army; Lear's limericks for comedy. Because English has many unstressed little words, anapaests come easily but can become sing-song. Anapaestic lines often mix in iambs, especially at the start, so that the rhythm runs in rising groups of two or three syllables. The effect is of speed and momentum, which is why the metre is used for rides, chases and comic narrative, from Browning's 'How They Brought the Good News from Ghent to Aix' to Lewis Carroll.

And his cohorts were gleaming in purple and gold;
examples.title: The Destruction of Sennacherib
examples.author: Lord Byron
examples.why: Byron's anapaestic tetrameter: the as-SYR-ian came DOWN like the WOLF on the FOLD.

examples.title: There was an Old Man with a beard

examples.why: The limerick's skipping anapaests.

terms.short: Repetition of the same word or phrase at the start of successive lines or clauses.
terms.long: Anaphora builds rhythm and emotion by insistence. The Psalms, the Beatitudes and political speeches use it; Blake's 'London' repeats 'In every'; Whitman's catalogues are bound together by it; and the hypnotic opening 'Gidiyorduk' of Yurdakul's 'Sürücü' does the same in Turkish. Anaphora is one of the oldest devices of poetry and oratory, found in Hebrew psalms, Greek hymns and medieval litanies. It can make a poem sound like prayer, protest or incantation, and it can bind together long lines that have no metre, as in Whitman.

lines: In every cry of every man,
In every infant's cry of fear,
examples.title: London
examples.author: William Blake
examples.why: Blake's insistent 'In every'.

terms.short: Turning aside to address someone absent or dead, or something not human, as if it could hear.
terms.long: 'O Rose, thou art sick!'; 'Milton! thou shouldst be living at this hour'; 'Death, be not proud'. Apostrophe is the gesture of the ode and the elegy, where the speaker calls on what cannot answer. It lends urgency and emotion, and can seem rhetorical; its very helplessness can also be moving. The word comes from the Greek for 'turning away': the speaker turns from the audience to address someone or something else. Apostrophe is common in odes, elegies, laments and prayers, and in drama in soliloquies addressed to absent persons or to the heavens.

lines: O rose, thou art sick!
The invisible worm,
examples.title: The Sick Rose

lines: It moves us not.—Great God! I’d rather be

examples.title: The World Is Too Much with Us
examples.author: William Wordsworth
examples.why: Wordsworth cries out to God and wishes he could see Proteus and Triton.

terms.short: A prose or verse summary placed before a poem or a book of a long poem.
terms.long: Renaissance editions often printed an 'argument' at the head of each book or canto, telling the reader what was to come. Milton added prose arguments to Paradise Lost in 1668; Chapman's Iliad has verse arguments; Spenser prefaces each canto with a quatrain. The Codex shows arguments but does not count them in line numbers. The word 'argument' here means subject, not dispute. Arguments help readers follow long and complicated poems, and they also show how a poem was presented by its author or editor. Milton's arguments, added after the first edition, explain his plan; Chapman's are themselves short poems in couplets.

examples.title: Paradise Lost · Book I
examples.author: John Milton
examples.why: The start of Milton's prose argument to Book I.

examples.title: The Iliad · Book I

terms.short: The quantitative metre of Arabic, Persian and Ottoman poetry, based on patterns of long and short syllables.
terms.long: Arabic prosody, codified by al-Khalil in the eighth century, measures lines by the length of syllables rather than by stress or by count. Persian adapted it, and Ottoman poets took it from Persian as aruz. Each metre is a fixed sequence of long and short syllables, and poets learned them through mnemonic words (fâ'ilâtün, mefâ'îlün). Turkish has few naturally long vowels, so writing in aruz meant leaning on Arabic and Persian vocabulary, one reason divan poetry became so learned. In the early twentieth century Turkish poets turned back to the native syllabic hece.

Çekildik izzet ü ikbal ile bab-ı hükûmetten
examples.title: Hürriyet Kasidesi
examples.author: Namık Kemal
examples.why: Namik Kemal's kaside, like the divan poetry it answers, is measured in aruz.

Sun and moon traverse the sphere in mystic dance.
examples.title: While the Lovers Circle Here in Mystic Dance
examples.author: Şeyh Galip
examples.why: Gibb imitates the steady beat of Galib's aruz in English.

terms.short: Repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words.
terms.long: Where alliteration repeats consonants at the start of words, assonance repeats vowels anywhere ('thou foster-child of silence and slow time'). It makes lines musical and binds them without rhyme; in some Spanish and Old French verse it replaces rhyme altogether. Assonance often works below conscious notice, giving a line a sense of unity or mood. Long vowels can slow a line and make it solemn; short vowels can quicken it. Together with alliteration and rhyme, it is one of the main ways sound binds words in a poem.

Thou foster-child of silence and slow time,
examples.title: Ode on a Grecian Urn
examples.author: John Keats
examples.why: The long o and i sounds of Keats's first lines.

terms.short: A poem of lovers parting at dawn, or one addressed to the morning.
terms.long: The Provençal alba and the German Tagelied were songs of lovers who must part when day breaks, often warned by a watchman or a bird. English poets made the form wittier: in Donne's 'The Sun Rising' the lover scolds the sun for interrupting. The word is also used of any morning poem. The dawn song depends on a simple situation that poets can turn many ways: the night has been too short, the lovers would stop time, and the world outside insists on its claims. Romeo and Juliet's quarrel over whether they hear the nightingale or the lark is a dramatic aubade.

lines: BUsie old foole, unruly Sunne,
Why dost thou thus,
examples.title: The Sunne Rising.
examples.author: John Donne
examples.why: Donne's lover rebukes the sun for calling at the window.

terms.short: A short story told in song-like stanzas, often anonymous, dramatic and tragic.
terms.long: The traditional ballads of England and Scotland were sung and passed on by ear for centuries before collectors wrote them down; Percy's Reliques (1765), Scott's Minstrelsy (1802-03) and Child's great edition (1882-98) preserved hundreds. A ballad tells a story quickly, often beginning in the middle, with little comment from the teller. It moves by dialogue, leaps between scenes, repeats lines and questions with small changes (incremental repetition), and favours sudden death, the supernatural and family feud. Most are in the ballad stanza. The Romantics imitated the form in literary ballads, and the Codex also holds many printed broadside ballads, sold on the street for a penny.

O where hae ye been, my handsome young man?’--
examples.title: Lord Randal

terms.short: A quatrain of alternating four-stress and three-stress lines, rhyming on the second and fourth lines.
terms.long: The usual stanza of the traditional ballads: four lines, the first and third with four beats and the second and fourth with three, rhymed abcb (sometimes abab). Its swing is easy to sing and remember. When the lines are strictly iambic with eight and six syllables, the same pattern is called common metre, the metre of many hymns. Coleridge used and stretched the ballad stanza in The Rime of the Ancient Mariner; Emily Dickinson built much of her work on its hymn-book cousin.

lines: The king sits in Dunfermline town
Drinking the blude-red wine;
examples.title: Sir Patrick Spens

examples.why: Coleridge opens his literary ballad in the same measure.

examples.why: Dickinson's lines alternate four and three beats like a ballad or hymn.

terms.short: A French form of three stanzas and an envoi on the same rhymes, each ending with the same refrain line.
terms.long: Not to be confused with the ballad. The ballade was a favourite of medieval French poets, Villon above all. Its three stanzas (often of eight lines, rhyming ababbcbc) use the same rhymes throughout, each ends with the refrain, and a short envoi, often addressed to a 'Prince', closes the poem. Chaucer wrote ballades; Rossetti and Swinburne translated Villon's; and late Victorian poets (Lang, Henley, Chesterton) wrote many, often comic.

Lady Flora the lovely Roman?
examples.title: The Ballad of Dead Ladies
examples.author: François Villon
examples.why: Rossetti's version of Villon's ballade of famous women, whose refrain asks where last year's snows are.

lines: The gallows in my garden, people say,
Is new and neat and adequately tall.
examples.title: A Ballade of Suicide
examples.author: G. K. Chesterton
examples.why: A comic ballade by Chesterton.

terms.short: Unrhymed iambic pentameter.
terms.long: Surrey first used blank verse in English for his translation of Books II and IV of the Aeneid (printed 1554-57), and Marlowe made it the voice of the Elizabethan stage. Shakespeare's plays, Milton's Paradise Lost, Wordsworth's Prelude and Tennyson's dramatic monologues are in blank verse. Free of rhyme, it can run its sense over from line to line in long paragraphs, which Milton called 'the sense variously drawn out from one verse into another', and can come close to the rhythm of speech.

terms.short: A catalogue of a beloved's beauties, part by part: hair, eyes, lips, neck.
terms.long: The term comes from heraldry, where to blazon is to describe a coat of arms. Petrarchan poets listed the lady's features with fixed comparisons (golden hair, coral lips, eyes like stars), and the blazon became a set piece of Renaissance love poetry. Shakespeare's Sonnet 130 is a famous anti-blazon that refuses the comparisons one by one. The blazon tends to divide the beloved into parts and to compare each to precious things: gold, ivory, pearls, rubies. Critics have pointed out that it can make the woman an object to be admired rather than a person, which is part of what Shakespeare's Sonnet 130 mocks.

terms.short: A pause or break within a line of verse.
terms.long: In classical and Old English verse the caesura falls at a fixed or customary point; in English pentameter it can come anywhere, marked by punctuation or by the sense, and its placement shapes the line's rhythm. Pope's couplets often balance around a central caesura; Milton moves it constantly. In Old English it divides the half-lines; in Turkish hece verse it is the durak.

terms.short: A major division of a long poem, like a chapter.
terms.long: From the Italian for 'song'. Dante divided the Divine Comedy into a hundred cantos; Ariosto, Tasso, Spenser and Byron used cantos too. Classical epics divide into books; Middle English romances into fitts; Piers Plowman into passus ('steps'). The Codex shows long works by their own divisions. Dividing a long poem in this way helps readers find their place and gives the poet natural pauses, often marked by new beginnings, summaries or invocations. A canto may be a few hundred lines or many more; in the Codex each canto, book, fitt or passus of a long work has a page of its own.

terms.short: The theme that life is short and pleasure, especially love, should be taken while it can.
terms.long: The phrase is from Horace (Odes 1.11): 'seize the day, trusting as little as possible to tomorrow'. Classical and Renaissance love poets used it to press a lover: beauty fades, time flies, the grave is cold. Herrick's 'To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time' and Marvell's 'To His Coy Mistress' are the famous English examples, the latter turning the argument into a mock-logical syllogism.

Old Time is still a flying:
examples.title: To the Virgins, to make much of Time.
examples.author: Robert Herrick
examples.why: Herrick's opening is the theme in a single image.

examples.author: Andrew Marvell
examples.why: Marvell's speaker begins with the leisurely love he would offer if there were time.

terms.short: A long list of people, places or things, a set piece of epic and of later poetry.
terms.long: The Catalogue of Ships in Iliad II lists the Greek contingents, their leaders and homes in hundreds of lines; Milton lists the fallen angels who became the gods of the nations. Catalogues show the poet's knowledge and the scale of the subject. Whitman turned the catalogue into a democratic embrace, listing the people and trades of America. A catalogue need not be dull: it can build momentum, create a sense of plenty or loss, and give a poem a public, inclusive scope. The Old English poem Widsith lists kings and peoples; Hesiod's Theogony lists gods; and the biblical genealogies are a related form.

examples.title: The Iliad · Book II
examples.author: Homer

lines: The pure contralto sings in the organ loft,
The carpenter dresses his plank, the tongue of his foreplane
examples.title: Song of Myself
examples.author: Walt Whitman
examples.why: Whitman's catalogue of Americans at work.

terms.short: A reversal of the order of words or ideas in two parallel phrases: A B, B A.
terms.long: Named after the Greek letter chi (X), whose shape traces the crossing. 'A wit with dunces, and a dunce with wits' (Pope). Chiasmus gives a line balance and closure and suits antithesis, which made it a favourite of the Augustan couplet. Chiasmus is common in proverbs and scripture ('the first shall be last, and the last first') and in oratory. In verse it lets a line or couplet close on itself, with the second half mirroring the first, so the idea seems complete and quotable.

A wit with dunces, and a dunce with wits.
examples.title: The Dunciad, Book IV
examples.author: Alexander Pope
examples.why: A wit with dunces, and a dunce with wits: the order of wit and dunce crosses in Pope's line.

terms.short: A quatrain of iambic lines of eight and six syllables, alternating, the metre of many hymns.
terms.long: Hymn books label their metres by syllable count, and 'common metre' (C.M., 8.6.8.6) is the commonest of all. It is the ballad stanza made regular: iambic tetrameter and trimeter lines in turn, rhyming abab or abcb. Isaac Watts wrote hundreds of hymns in it, and the congregation could sing any of them to any common-metre tune. Emily Dickinson grew up with Watts's hymns, and her poems use common metre and its relatives (short metre, 6.6.8.6; long metre, 8.8.8.8) while bending their rhymes and dashes against the familiar beat.

He kindly stopped for me;
examples.title: Because I could not stop for Death
examples.author: Emily Dickinson
examples.why: Eight syllables, then six: Dickinson's poem moves in common metre.

There's none hath power divine;
examples.title: Psalm 86: A general song of praise to God

examples.why: A psalm of praise by Isaac Watts, who made the metre the standard of English hymn singing.

terms.short: An ingenious, far-fetched comparison worked out at length.
terms.long: A conceit is a metaphor that draws attention to its own cleverness. The Petrarchan conceit (the lover freezing and burning, the lady's eyes as suns) became a stock of Elizabethan love poetry. The metaphysical poets, Donne above all, made conceits of startling learning and argument: two lovers' souls as the legs of a pair of compasses, a flea as a marriage bed. Dr Johnson complained that in such poems 'the most heterogeneous ideas are yoked by violence together'.

lines: If they be two, they are two so
As stiffe twin compasses are two,
examples.title: A Valediction: forbidding mourning
examples.author: John Donne
examples.why: Donne begins his comparison of parted lovers to a pair of compasses.

How little that which thou deny'st me is;
examples.title: The Flea.
examples.author: John Donne
examples.why: Donne's flea, in which the lovers' blood is already mingled.

terms.short: Two lines that go together, usually rhyming and of the same length.
terms.long: The couplet is the smallest stanza. It can stand alone as an epigram, close a sonnet or a scene of a play, or run on, couplet after couplet, through a long poem. Chaucer's Canterbury Tales is largely in pentameter couplets; Marvell's 'To His Coy Mistress' in tetrameter couplets; Pope perfected the closed heroic couplet. In the ghazal and the mesnevi the couplet (beyit) is the basic unit, though with different rules of rhyme.

lines: HAD we but World enough, and Time,
This coyness Lady were no crime.
examples.title: To his Coy Mistress.
examples.author: Andrew Marvell
examples.why: Marvell's tetrameter couplets, eight syllables a line.

lines: So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
examples.title: Sonnet 18
examples.author: William Shakespeare
examples.why: The couplet that closes Sonnet 18.

terms.short: A metrical foot of a stressed syllable followed by two unstressed ones: DUM-de-de.
terms.long: The dactyl (from the Greek for 'finger', with its one long and two short joints) is the foot of the Greek and Latin epic hexameter. In English, dactylic rhythm is falling and rapid: Tennyson's 'Charge of the Light Brigade' uses it to imitate hoofbeats, and Longfellow's Evangeline imitates the classical dactylic hexameter. Dactylic rhythm falls away from its stress, and in English it often ends a line on a stressed syllable, cutting off the final weak syllables. Sustained dactyls are hard to keep up in English, which has relatively few words of that shape, so many 'dactylic' poems mix the foot freely with trochees.

lines: HALF a league, half a league,
Half a league onward,
examples.title: The Charge of the Light Brigade
examples.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
examples.why: HALF a league, HALF a league: two dactyls.

lines: This is the forest primeval.  The murmuring pines and the hemlocks,
Bearded with moss, and in garments green, indistinct in the twilight,
examples.title: Evangeline · Prelude
examples.author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
examples.why: Longfellow's dactylic hexameter.

terms.short: A poem spoken by a character, not the poet, to a silent listener, revealing more than the speaker intends.
terms.long: The form was perfected by Robert Browning and Tennyson in the 1840s. A single speaker, at a particular moment, addresses someone whose replies we infer; the reader pieces together the situation and the character from what is said, and often sees through the speaker. In Browning's 'My Last Duchess' a duke shows a portrait of his late wife to an envoy and lets slip that he had her killed. The form suits irony and the exploration of minds unlike the poet's own.

lines: That's my last Duchess painted on the wall,
Looking as if she were alive. I call
examples.title: My Last Duchess
examples.author: Robert Browning
examples.why: The Duke begins by drawing attention to a painting of his late wife.

lines: Much the same smile?  This grew; I gave commands;
Then all smiles stopped together. There she stands
examples.title: My Last Duchess
examples.author: Robert Browning
examples.why: Two of the poem's most chilling lines, spoken as if in passing.

lines: It little profits that an idle king,
By this still hearth, among these barren crags,
examples.title: Ulysses
examples.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
examples.why: Tennyson's aged Ulysses speaks of his restlessness on Ithaca.

terms.short: A poem in which the narrator falls asleep and dreams the poem's events, often an allegory.
terms.long: A favourite medieval frame: the poet wanders out, often on a May morning, falls asleep, and dreams of a garden, a guide, a debate or a revelation, then wakes to write it down. The Romance of the Rose, Chaucer's Book of the Duchess and Parliament of Fowls, Langland's Piers Plowman and Pearl are dream visions; The Dream of the Rood is an earlier Old English one. The dream licenses the marvellous and invites allegorical reading.

lines: Lo, I shall tell you the truest of visions,
A dream that I dreamt in the dead of night
examples.title: The Dream of the Rood
examples.author: Anonymous (Old English)
examples.why: In The Dream of the Rood the dreamer sees the Cross itself, which speaks.
examples.translator: trans. Cosette Faust Newton & Stith Thompson (1918)

lines: What this mountaigne by-meneth
And the merke dale,
examples.title: Piers Plowman · Passus I
examples.author: William Langland
examples.why: In Piers Plowman a lady explains the meaning of the dreamer's vision of the field full of folk.

terms.short: A vivid description of a work of art, real or imagined, in words.
terms.long: The first great ekphrasis is the Shield of Achilles in Iliad XVIII, where Homer describes the scenes Hephaestus forges on it: cities at peace and war, harvest and dance. Keats's 'Ode on a Grecian Urn' questions the figures on an urn; Browning's duke shows off a portrait. Ekphrasis lets a poem reflect on art, stillness and time. Ekphrasis invites readers to imagine an object they cannot see and often makes the work of art speak or come alive. It raises questions about the differences between visual art, which shows a single moment, and poetry, which unfolds in time, a contrast Keats explores in his Grecian Urn.

lines: What men or gods are these? What maidens loth?
What mad pursuit? What struggle to escape?
examples.title: Ode on a Grecian Urn
examples.author: John Keats
examples.why: Keats asks who the figures on the urn are.

lines: That's my last Duchess painted on the wall,
Looking as if she were alive. I call
examples.title: My Last Duchess
examples.author: Robert Browning
examples.why: Browning's poem begins before a painting.

terms.short: In Greek and Latin verse, a dactylic hexameter followed by a shorter 'pentameter'.
terms.long: The elegiac couplet was the classical metre for elegy, epigram and love poetry: Ovid, Propertius, Tibullus and the Greek epigrammatists wrote in it. The first line is a full hexameter; the second, the so-called pentameter, falls in two halves, each ending on a strong syllable, so that the couplet seems to rise and fall back. English imitations are rare but Coleridge made a famous one describing the metre in its own rhythm.

lines: In the hexameter rises the fountain's silvery column;
In the pentameter aye falling in melody back.
examples.title: The Ovidian Elegiac Metre Described and Exemplified
examples.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
examples.why: Coleridge describes the elegiac couplet in an elegiac couplet.

terms.short: A poem of mourning, for a person or for something lost, that often moves towards consolation.
terms.long: In Greek and Latin an elegy was any poem in elegiac couplets, on love as often as on death. In English the word came to mean a poem of lament, and by extension any meditative poem on mortality and loss. A formal elegy commonly passes through grief, praise of the dead and questioning towards some consolation, whether religious, natural or in the survival of memory and art. Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard (1751) mourns no one person but the forgotten poor; Tennyson's In Memoriam (1850) spends seventeen years of doubt on one friend. The Old English poems such as The Wanderer are often called elegies too.

lines: The curfew tolls the knell of parting day,
The lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea,
examples.title: Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard
examples.author: Thomas Gray
examples.why: Gray's elegy begins at dusk in a country churchyard.

lines: FAREWELL, thou child of my right hand, and joy;
My sin was too much hope of thee, loved boy;
examples.title: On my First Son
examples.author: Ben Jonson
examples.why: Jonson's short elegy for his son, dead at seven.

lines: Often the lonely one longs for honors,
The grace of God, though, grieved in his soul,
examples.title: The Wanderer
examples.author: Anonymous (Old English)
examples.why: The Wanderer, one of the Old English poems known as elegies.
examples.translator: trans. Cosette Faust Newton & Stith Thompson (1918)

terms.short: A line whose sense and syntax pause at its end, usually marked by punctuation.
terms.long: End-stopping gives verse a measured, definite quality: each line is a unit of thought. It is characteristic of the Augustan heroic couplet, where each line and each couplet often closes on a comma, semicolon or full stop. Early Elizabethan blank verse is mostly end-stopped; Shakespeare's later verse and Milton's are increasingly enjambed. A poem of end-stopped lines can sound formal, epigrammatic or incantatory; too many can sound stiff. Pope balanced this by varying the caesura inside his lines and by running a sentence over two or more couplets when he wished. Many poets alternate end-stopped and run-on lines to shape the rhythm of a passage.

lines: A little learning is a dangerous thing;
Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring:
examples.title: An Essay on Criticism
examples.author: Alexander Pope
examples.why: Each line of Pope's couplet ends with a pause.

terms.short: The running-on of a sentence from one line into the next without a pause at the line's end.
terms.long: When sense and syntax carry past the end of a line, the line-break creates suspense, emphasis or surprise: the reader's eye must leap to finish the thought. Milton's blank verse is full of enjambment, his sentences flowing over many lines. Its opposite is the end-stopped line. Enjambment across stanzas is rarer and more striking. Enjambment can be gentle, simply carrying a sentence forward, or sharp, splitting a phrase so that the line-break creates a second meaning or a moment of suspense. Paradise Lost begins with a sentence that runs across sixteen lines, and much of its power comes from the way its sense keeps running over the line ends.

lines: Of Mans First Disobedience, and the Fruit
Of that Forbidden Tree, whose mortal tast
examples.title: Paradise Lost · Book I
examples.author: John Milton
examples.why: Milton's opening sentence runs on for six lines before its verb, 'Sing'.

lines: Then felt I like some watcher of the skies
When a new planet swims into his ken;
examples.title: On First Looking into Chapman's Homer
examples.author: John Keats
examples.why: Keats runs his sense over into the next line.

terms.short: A short closing stanza that sends the poem on its way, often addressing a patron or the reader.
terms.long: From the French for 'sending'. The ballade ends with an envoi of four or five lines, traditionally beginning 'Prince'; the sestina ends with a three-line envoi that uses all six end-words. Chaucer's short poems end with envois to friends and to King Henry IV ('O conquerour of Brutes Albioun'). Any closing address to the book or the reader can be called an envoi.

lines: O conquerour of Brutes Albioun!
Which that by lyne and free eleccioun
examples.title: The Complaint of Chaucer to His Purse
examples.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
examples.why: Chaucer's complaint to his empty purse ends with an envoi to the new king, Henry IV, hoping for payment.

lines: Therfore, thou vache, leve thyn old wrecchednesse
Unto the worlde; leve now to be thral;
examples.title: Truth (Balade de Bon Conseyl)
examples.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
examples.why: The envoi to 'Truth', addressed to a friend, perhaps Sir Philip de la Vache.

terms.short: A long narrative poem in an elevated style about heroic deeds that matter to a whole people.
terms.long: The epic tells of heroes, wars, journeys and the founding of nations, often with gods taking part. Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, oral poems composed in Greek hexameters, set the pattern; Virgil's Aeneid made it a written, literary form; Milton's Paradise Lost turned it to the fall of man. Epics share conventions: an opening statement of theme and an invocation of the Muse, a beginning in the middle of the action, catalogues of warriors and ships, extended similes, set speeches, fixed epithets, and journeys to the underworld. Other traditions have their own epics: Gilgamesh, the Mahabharata, Beowulf, the Shahnameh, the Kalevala.

lines: Achilles’ wrath, to Greece the direful spring
Of woes unnumber’d, heavenly goddess, sing!
examples.title: The Iliad · Book I
examples.author: Homer
examples.why: Pope's Iliad opens by naming its subject, the anger of Achilles, and calling on the goddess.

lines: Of Mans First Disobedience, and the Fruit
Of that Forbidden Tree, whose mortal tast
examples.title: Paradise Lost · Book I
examples.author: John Milton
examples.why: Milton announces a subject greater than Homer's.

lines: LO, praise of the prowess of people-kings
of spear-armed Danes, in days long sped,
examples.title: Beowulf · Prelude of the Founder of the Danish House
examples.author: Beowulf Poet
examples.why: Gummere's Beowulf begins with a call to hear of the Danish kings of old.

terms.short: A long, elaborate comparison, developed for several lines, often drawn from nature or daily life.
terms.long: Homer interrupts his battles with similes that open a window on another world: a warrior falls like a poplar felled by a wheelwright, the Greek army gathers like flies round milk-pails in spring. The comparison grows beyond its starting point into a small scene of its own, and returns, 'so' or 'even so', to the action. Virgil and Milton imitated the device; Milton's fallen angels lie 'thick as autumnal leaves' in the brooks of Vallombrosa and his Satan's shield hangs like the moon seen through Galileo's telescope.

lines: Thick as Autumnal Leaves that strow the Brooks
In Vallombrosa, where th' Etrurian shades
examples.title: Paradise Lost · Book I
examples.author: John Milton
examples.why: Milton's fallen angels, compared to fallen leaves in an Italian valley.

lines: Hung on his shoulders like the Moon, whose Orb
Through Optic Glass the Tuscan Artist views
examples.title: Paradise Lost · Book I
examples.author: John Milton
examples.why: Satan's shield, compared to the moon seen through Galileo's telescope.

lines: As from some rocky cleft the shepherd sees
Clustering in heaps on heaps the driving bees,
examples.title: The Iliad · Book II
examples.author: Homer
examples.why: Pope's Iliad, Book II: the Greeks pour out to assembly like bees from a rock.

terms.short: A short, pointed poem, often witty or satirical, ending with a sting.
terms.long: In Greek an epigram was simply an inscription, and the Greek Anthology collects thousands. Martial, in first-century Rome, made the epigram sharp and satirical, and it is his kind that English poets from Jonson to Pope imitated: a few lines, often a couplet or two, building to a final turn of wit. Coleridge defined it in an epigram of his own as a 'dwarfish whole', its body brevity and its soul wit.

lines: What is an Epigram? a dwarfish whole,
Its body brevity, and wit its soul.
examples.title: Epigram: What is an Epigram? a dwarfish whole
examples.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
examples.why: Coleridge's definition of the form, itself an epigram.

lines: These who with fame eternal their own dear land endowed
Took on them as a mantle the shade of death's dark cloud;
examples.title: On the Spartans
examples.author: Simonides of Ceos
examples.why: A Greek epigram in the older sense: an inscription in verse.

terms.short: A short inscription for a tomb, or a poem written as if for one.
terms.long: Greek epitaphs were carved in stone, and their brevity became an art: a name, a fact, a plea to the passer-by. The Greek Anthology holds hundreds, including the lines on the Spartans at Thermopylae attributed to Simonides. English poets wrote epitaphs both to be carved and to be read, solemn or satirical. Many epitaphs speak in the voice of the dead or address the traveller ('Stranger', 'Go tell'), and many are epigrams in form.

lines: These who with fame eternal their own dear land endowed
Took on them as a mantle the shade of death's dark cloud;
examples.title: On the Spartans
examples.author: Simonides of Ceos
examples.why: The famous epitaph for the Spartans who fell at Thermopylae, in an English version.

lines: Rest in soft peace, and, asked, say here doth lie
Ben Jonson his best piece of poetry;
examples.title: On my First Son
examples.author: Ben Jonson
examples.why: Jonson's poem on his son ends as an inscription for the grave.

terms.short: A poem celebrating a wedding, traditionally sung to the bride and groom on their way to the marriage chamber.
terms.long: From the Greek for 'at the bridal chamber'. Sappho wrote wedding songs, and Catullus gave the form its classical shape. Its conventions include the procession, the praise of the bride, the invocation of Hymen, god of marriage, and wishes for the night and for children. Spenser's Epithalamion (1595), written for his own wedding and closing his Amoretti, follows the hours of the wedding day, with a refrain about the woods answering and the echo ringing.

lines: The woods shall to me answer, and my Eccho ring.
Early, before the worlds light-giving lampe
examples.title: Epithalamion
examples.author: Edmund Spenser
examples.why: The refrain of Spenser's wedding poem, changing slightly through the day.

lines: HAile Bishop Valentine, whose day this is,
All the Aire is thy Diocis,
examples.title: An Epithalamion, Or mariage Song on the Lady Elizabeth, and Count Palatine being married on St. Valentines day.
examples.author: John Donne
examples.why: Donne's epithalamion for Princess Elizabeth's wedding on St Valentine's Day 1613.

terms.short: A descriptive word or phrase attached to a name: 'swift-footed Achilles', 'rosy-fingered Dawn'.
terms.long: Homer's characters and things carry fixed epithets that recur whenever they are named: 'grey-eyed Athena', 'the wine-dark sea'. In oral composition such formulas, fitted to different parts of the hexameter line, helped the singer compose as he performed. English poets imitated them, and Old English poetry has its own compounds, close to kennings. A transferred epithet attaches a quality to the wrong word ('a sleepless night').

lines: His prise to me.” To this replied the swift-foot, god-like, son
Of Thetis, thus: “King of us all, in all ambition
examples.title: The Iliad · Book I
examples.author: Homer
examples.why: Chapman keeps Homer's epithet for Achilles, 'swift-footed'.

lines: And when the lady of the light, the rosy-finger’d Morn,
Rose from the hills, all fresh arose, and to the camp retir’d.
examples.title: The Iliad · Book I
examples.author: Homer
examples.why: The most famous Homeric epithet, for the Dawn.

terms.short: An extra unstressed syllable at the end of a line.
terms.long: An iambic pentameter line normally ends on a stress; a feminine ending adds a light syllable after it ('To be, or not to be: that is the QUES-tion'). Shakespeare used more feminine endings as his career went on, making his verse more conversational. Feminine rhyme is the matching two-syllable rhyme (painted/acquainted), which Shakespeare's Sonnet 20 uses throughout. The names 'masculine' and 'feminine' come from French prosody, where they referred to grammatical gender and the silent final e; they are traditional, not a judgement. Feminine endings soften a line's close and make blank verse more like speech, and in rhyme they are often used for comic effect, as in Byron's Don Juan.

lines: To be, or not to be, that is the question:
Whether ’tis nobler in the mind to suffer
examples.title: The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark · Act III, Scene 1
examples.author: William Shakespeare
examples.why: Hamlet's line ends with the unstressed '-tion'.

lines: A woman's face with nature's own hand painted,
Hast thou, the master mistress of my passion;
examples.title: Sonnet 20
examples.author: William Shakespeare
examples.why: Every line of Sonnet 20 has a feminine ending.

terms.short: The unit of metre: a group of stressed and unstressed (or long and short) syllables.
terms.long: The common feet in English are the iamb (de-DUM), the trochee (DUM-de), the anapaest (de-de-DUM), the dactyl (DUM-de-de) and the spondee (DUM-DUM). A line is named by its foot and the number of feet: three is trimeter, four tetrameter, five pentameter, six hexameter. The terms are borrowed from Greek and Latin, where they described syllable length, not stress. Feet are a convenient description rather than a law of nature: in reading aloud we do not pause between them, and many lines can be divided in more than one way. Still, naming the feet helps a reader hear where a poet has kept to the pattern and where the rhythm departs from it for effect.

lines: Tyger, tyger, burning bright
In the forests of the night,
examples.title: The Tyger
examples.author: William Blake
examples.why: Blake's line falls into trochees: TY-ger TY-ger BURN-ing BRIGHT.

terms.short: A line of fourteen syllables, seven iambic feet, often rhymed in couplets.
terms.long: The fourteener was popular in the sixteenth century, used for translations of Ovid (Golding, 1567) and Seneca, and by George Chapman for his Iliad (1598-1611), which Keats read with such excitement. Broken at the caesura, a fourteener couplet becomes a ballad stanza of four and three beats. The line's length gives it a rolling, narrative energy, but in English it tends to break at the eighth syllable, which is why printers later set many fourteener poems as ballad stanzas. Chapman's Iliad, despite its roughness, kept a reputation for vigour: Keats's sonnet on first reading it is one of the Codex's sonnet examples.

lines: Achilles’ baneful wrath resound, O Goddess, that impos’d
Infinite sorrows on the Greeks, and many brave souls los’d.
examples.title: The Iliad · Book I
examples.author: Homer
examples.why: Chapman's Iliad opens in rhymed fourteeners.

lines: Of shapes transformde to bodies straunge, I purpose to entreate,
Ye gods vouchsafe (for you are they ywrought this wondrous feate)
examples.title: Metamorphoses (Golding) · Book I
examples.author: Ovid
examples.why: Golding's Ovid, the other great Elizabethan translation in fourteeners.

terms.short: Verse without regular metre or rhyme, shaped by the rhythm of phrases and the placing of line-breaks.
terms.long: Free verse does not count syllables or beats. Its lines follow breath, syntax and emphasis, and its music comes from repetition, parallelism and cadence. The King James Bible's psalms and Macpherson's Ossian prepared the way; Walt Whitman's Leaves of Grass (1855) made it a major mode in English, and French symbolists and then the Imagists made vers libre the common form of modern poetry.

lines: I celebrate myself, and sing myself,
And what I assume you shall assume,
examples.title: Song of Myself
examples.author: Walt Whitman
examples.why: Whitman's long lines follow the rhythm of statement, not metre.

lines: When lilacs last in the dooryard bloom’d,
And the great star early droop’d in the western sky in the night,
examples.title: When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d
examples.author: Walt Whitman
examples.why: The opening of Whitman's elegy for Lincoln.

terms.short: The Ottoman Turkish ghazal: a short love lyric of monorhymed couplets in quantitative metre.
terms.long: In Ottoman divan poetry the gazel was the chief lyric form, usually of five to twelve beyits in aruz metre, rhyming aa ba ca and so on, often with a redif. Fuzuli in the sixteenth century, Baki, Nedim in the Tulip Age and Seyh Galib in the late eighteenth are its masters. A poet's divan (collected poems) was arranged with gazels in alphabetical order of their rhymes. The beloved, the wine-cup, the rose and nightingale and the candle and moth are its stock images, made new by wit and feeling. Later writers sometimes wrote a nazire, a poem answering another poet's gazel in the same rhyme and metre.

lines: While the lovers circle here in mystic dance,
Sun and moon traverse the sphere in mystic dance.
examples.title: While the Lovers Circle Here in Mystic Dance
examples.author: Şeyh Galip
examples.why: Gibb keeps Galib's redif, 'in mystic dance', at the end of every couplet.

lines: But a glass or two she gave us, yet she drave our thoughts astray;
Out on yonder wine-retailing, wit-assailing paynim may!
examples.title: But a Glass or Two She Gave Us
examples.author: Nedim
examples.why: A gazel by Nedim, poet of the Tulip Age.

lines: Gözlerim bir dilsitânıñ vâlih ü hayrânıdır
Bir melek mihmânserâ-yı sinemiñ mihmânıdır
examples.title: Nazîre-i Gazel-i Muallim
examples.author: Cenap Şahabettin
examples.why: A late Ottoman nazire, written in reply to another poet's gazel.

terms.short: A poem that teaches a practical art, especially farming, named after Virgil's Georgics.
terms.long: Hesiod's Works and Days, with its calendar of farm work and its warnings, and Virgil's Georgics (29 BC), on crops, trees, livestock and bees, are the classical models. The georgic gives instruction in verse but also praises labour, the seasons and the countryside. Eighteenth-century English poets took it up eagerly, writing georgics on cider, sheep, sugar cane and hop-gardens; Thomson's The Seasons draws on it too. The Codex lists such poems as 'didactic poems'.

lines: WHat makes a plenteous Harvest, when to turn
The fruitful Soil, and when to sowe the Corn;
examples.title: The Georgics · Book I
examples.author: Virgil
examples.why: Dryden's translation of the first Georgic, on ploughing and the weather.

lines: If thou, O Hesiod! Virgil of our land,
Or hear'st thou rather, Milton, bard divine,
examples.title: The Hop-Garden · Book I
examples.author: Christopher Smart
examples.why: Christopher Smart's georgic on growing hops in Kent calls on Hesiod and Virgil as its masters.

terms.short: A lyric of self-contained couplets on one rhyme, often with a repeated word after it, and the poet's name in the last couplet.
terms.long: The ghazal began in Arabic and became the central lyric form of Persian, Ottoman Turkish and Urdu poetry. It is made of couplets (Persian bayt, Turkish beyit), usually five to fifteen. Both lines of the first couplet rhyme; thereafter the second line of each couplet keeps the same rhyme, often followed by a refrain word or phrase (radif, Turkish redif). Each couplet is complete in itself, yet the poem holds together by mood and image: love, longing, wine, the beloved's cruelty, which may also be read as love of God. In the final couplet the poet often names himself by his pen name (takhallus, Turkish mahlas). English translators rarely keep the single rhyme, but some, such as Gibb, tried.

lines: Strange if beauties' hearts turn blood through envy of thy cheek most fair?
For that which stone to ruby turns is but the radiant sunlight's glare.
examples.title: Strange If Beauties' Hearts Turn Blood
examples.author: Fuzuli
examples.why: Gibb keeps Fuzuli's single rhyme (-air) through every couplet of this gazel.

lines: Within her ward, with garments rent, on all sides rosy-cheeked ones stray;
Fuzûlî, through those radiant hues, that quarter beams a garden fair.
examples.title: Strange If Beauties' Hearts Turn Blood
examples.author: Fuzuli
examples.why: In the last couplet the poet names himself: 'Fuzuli'.

lines: To Thee, first,
From the clouds of Whose mercy is born
examples.title: Ghazal I
examples.author: Zeb-un-Nissa (Makhfi)
examples.why: A ghazal by the Mughal princess Zeb-un-Nissa, in an English stanza.
examples.translator: trans. Magan Lal and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1913)

terms.short: One of the two halves of a line of Old English alliterative verse, divided by the caesura.
terms.long: Editors of Old English print each line with a gap in the middle, and scholars call the halves the a-verse (on-verse) and the b-verse (off-verse). Each half-line has two stressed positions and follows one of a small number of rhythmic types (Sievers' five types). In Greek and Latin and in Ottoman poetry the half of a line is called a hemistich (Turkish mısra is a whole line, half a beyit).

lines: Hwæt! We Gardena    in geardagum,
þeodcyninga,    þrym gefrunon,
examples.title: Beowulf (Old English) · Lines 1–125
examples.author: Beowulf Poet
examples.why: The space in the printed text marks the division between the half-lines.

lines: What this mountaigne by-meneth
And the merke dale,
examples.title: Piers Plowman · Passus I
examples.author: William Langland
examples.why: This edition of Piers Plowman prints each half-line separately.

terms.short: The syllabic metre of Turkish folk poetry, which counts the syllables in a line, with a fixed pause.
terms.long: Turkish folk poets, the asiks and the anonymous makers of türkü and mani, measured their lines by counting syllables (hece), not by long and short. Lines of seven, eight and eleven syllables are commonest, divided by a pause (durak) at a fixed place, and stanzas are usually quatrains. At the end of the Ottoman period, nationalist poets such as Mehmet Emin Yurdakul championed hece as the truly Turkish measure against the Persian aruz, and in the 1910s the 'Five Syllabists' made it the metre of modern Turkish verse before free verse took over.

lines: Gidiyorduk: Kar üstünde bir incecik çığırdan;
Gidiyorduk: İri buzlar sarkıtmıştı her saçak;
examples.title: Sürücü
examples.author: Mehmet Emin Yurdakul
examples.why: Yurdakul's 'Sürücü' counts fifteen syllables a line, with a pause after the first word.

terms.short: A pair of rhymed iambic pentameter lines, often complete in sense, the staple of Augustan verse.
terms.long: Called 'heroic' because Dryden and others used it for heroic poetry and plays, the form goes back to Chaucer. In the hands of Dryden and Pope it became a closed unit: each couplet a complete statement, often balanced around the caesura and turning on antithesis, so that a long poem advances by a series of polished, quotable steps. Pope used it for translation (his Iliad), argument (An Essay on Man), satire and mock-epic. The Romantics, Keats in Endymion for instance, loosened it again with run-on lines.

lines: Achilles’ wrath, to Greece the direful spring
Of woes unnumber’d, heavenly goddess, sing!
examples.title: The Iliad · Book I
examples.author: Homer
examples.why: Pope's Iliad in heroic couplets.

lines: A little learning is a dangerous thing;
Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring:
examples.title: An Essay on Criticism
examples.author: Alexander Pope
examples.why: Pope's famous warning from An Essay on Criticism, a closed couplet.

lines: True ease in writing comes from art, not chance,
As those move easiest who have learn'd to dance.
examples.title: An Essay on Criticism
examples.author: Alexander Pope
examples.why: Pope's lines on making sound echo sense.

terms.short: A line of six feet; in Greek and Latin, the dactylic metre of epic.
terms.long: Homer, Hesiod, Virgil, Lucretius and Ovid's Metamorphoses are in dactylic hexameter: six feet, the first four dactyls or spondees, the fifth usually a dactyl, the last two syllables. English poets have tried to imitate it with stresses: Longfellow's Evangeline, Clough's Bothie, Kingsley's Andromeda. In English, an iambic line of six feet is usually called an alexandrine. In the classical hexameter a pause usually falls in the third foot, and the line's last two feet (a dactyl and a spondee or trochee) give its distinctive cadence, which Coleridge's example imitates: 'limitless billows'. Many English translators of Homer chose blank verse, couplets or fourteeners instead, finding the English hexameter monotonous.

lines: Strongly it bears us along in swelling and limitless billows,
Nothing before and nothing behind but the sky and the ocean.
examples.title: The Homeric Hexameter Described and Exemplified
examples.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
examples.why: Coleridge describes and imitates the Homeric hexameter.

lines: This is the forest primeval.  The murmuring pines and the hemlocks,
Bearded with moss, and in garments green, indistinct in the twilight,
examples.title: Evangeline · Prelude
examples.author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
examples.why: Longfellow's English hexameters.

terms.short: An ode on the model of Horace, calm and reflective, repeating one stanza throughout.
terms.long: Horace (65-8 BC) wrote his Odes in short, regular stanzas borrowed from Greek lyric (the Alcaic and the Sapphic among them). Where the Pindaric ode is public and soaring, the Horatian is restrained and thoughtful, often addressed to a friend. English poets imitated it with regular stanzas of their own. Marvell's 'An Horatian Ode upon Cromwell's Return from Ireland' (1650) is the classic example; Keats's odes, with their repeated ten-line stanza, stand in the same tradition.

lines: If aught of oaten stop, or pastoral song,
May hope, chaste Eve, to soothe thy modest ear,
examples.title: Ode to Evening
examples.author: William Collins
examples.why: Collins's 'Ode to Evening' keeps one quiet stanza throughout, modelled on Horace's.

terms.short: A song of praise, especially to God or a god, often written for singing by a congregation.
terms.long: The Greek hymns, such as the Homeric Hymns, praised the gods and told their stories. Christian hymns in Latin were sung in church from the fourth century. The English congregational hymn flourished from the early eighteenth century, when Isaac Watts and then Charles Wesley wrote thousands of hymns in plain metres anyone could sing. The Codex marks a poem as a hymn when its title says so, from Babylonian and Egyptian hymns to the sun to Victorian hymns for every occasion.

lines: Among the princes, earthly gods,
There's none hath power divine;
examples.title: Psalm 86: A general song of praise to God
examples.author: Isaac Watts
examples.why: A song of praise by Isaac Watts, in the regular stanzas of congregational singing.

terms.short: Deliberate exaggeration for emphasis or effect.
terms.long: Love poetry lives on hyperbole: the lover will love till the seas run dry, the lady's beauty outshines the sun. Marvell's coy mistress is promised a hundred years for praising her eyes and thirty thousand for the rest. Hyperbole can be passionate, comic or both. Exaggeration is not a lie because the reader knows it is not meant literally; its purpose is to convey the strength of feeling. In epic and romance it magnifies heroes and battles; in satire and comedy it exposes folly by blowing it up to absurd size.

lines: An hundred years should go to praise
Thine Eyes, and on thy Forehead Gaze.
examples.title: To his Coy Mistress.
examples.author: Andrew Marvell
examples.why: Marvell's exaggerated time-scheme of praise.

lines: Till a’ the seas gang dry.
Till a’ the seas gang dry, my dear,
examples.title: A Red, Red Rose
examples.author: Robert Burns
examples.why: Burns's lover promises to love till the seas dry up.

terms.short: A metrical foot of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one: de-DUM.
terms.long: The iamb is the natural rhythm of much English speech ('a-BOUT', 'the SUN'), and most English verse from Chaucer to the nineteenth century is iambic. Iambic pentameter is the line of the sonnet, blank verse and the heroic couplet; iambic tetrameter is lighter and quicker. Because the iamb rises to its stress, an iambic line tends to move forward and end firmly. Poets vary it constantly so that it does not become monotonous: a trochee at the start of the line, two light syllables together, or an extra syllable at the end. Shakespeare's verse is iambic but rarely mechanical.

lines: Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
examples.title: Sonnet 18
examples.author: William Shakespeare
examples.why: Shakespeare's line opens with a variation, then settles: com-PARE thee TO a SUM-mer's DAY.

terms.short: A line of five iambic feet, ten syllables: the main line of English verse.
terms.long: De-DUM five times. Chaucer established it in English, and it became the line of the sonnet, blank verse, the heroic couplet, rhyme royal and the Spenserian stanza. Its length suits a phrase and a half of speech, and it is rarely perfectly regular: poets invert the first foot, add a feminine ending, place the caesura anywhere, or let stresses fall unevenly, and the reader hears the variation against the pattern.

lines: Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
examples.title: Sonnet 18
examples.author: William Shakespeare
examples.why: Shakespeare's pentameter line.

lines: The curfew tolls the knell of parting day,
The lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea,
examples.title: Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard
examples.author: Thomas Gray
examples.why: Gray's slow, regular pentameter.

terms.short: Beginning a story in the middle of the action, and filling in what came before later.
terms.long: Horace praised Homer for hurrying his reader 'into the middle of things'. The Iliad begins in the tenth year of the war; the Odyssey with Odysseus already long away from home, his earlier wanderings told later at the Phaeacian court. Epics after Homer followed: Paradise Lost begins with Satan already fallen into Hell, and the war in Heaven is narrated by Raphael in the middle books. Milton's own argument to Book I says the poem 'hastes into the midst of things'.

into Hell describ'd here, not in the Center (for Heaven and Earth may be
examples.title: Paradise Lost · Book I
examples.author: John Milton
examples.why: Milton's prose argument names the convention.

terms.short: Rhyme within a line, or between a word inside a line and the line's end.
terms.long: Internal rhyme speeds a line and makes it chime. Coleridge's 'The fair breeze blew, the white foam flew' and Poe's 'The Raven' ('Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary') are famous examples; ballads often rhyme in the middle of the long line. Internal rhyme can come at the caesura, where the middle of a line rhymes with its end, or scattered through a line, where it produces a dense, chiming music. Poe used it to create a hypnotic effect; comic poets such as W. S. Gilbert used it for speed and fun.

lines: Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary,
Over many a quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore--
examples.title: The Raven
examples.author: Edgar Allan Poe
examples.why: Poe's first line rhymes dreary with weary inside the line.

lines: The fair breeze blew, the white foam flew,
The furrow followed free;
examples.title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
examples.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
examples.why: Blew and flew chime inside the Mariner's line.

terms.short: A poet's call to a Muse or god for help and inspiration, usually at the start of an epic.
terms.long: 'Sing, goddess, the wrath of Achilles'; 'Tell me, Muse, of the man of many ways'. The epic opens by naming its subject and asking a divine power to tell it, so that the poet becomes the Muse's voice. Milton invokes the 'Heav'nly Muse' who inspired Moses, and asks for help to soar above the classical poets; Spenser calls on Clio. Later poets used the convention playfully or replaced the Muse with other powers.

lines: Achilles’ wrath, to Greece the direful spring
Of woes unnumber’d, heavenly goddess, sing!
examples.title: The Iliad · Book I
examples.author: Homer
examples.why: Pope's version of Homer's opening call to the goddess.

lines: Sing Heav'nly Muse, that on the secret top
Of Oreb, or of Sinai, didst inspire
examples.title: Paradise Lost · Book I
examples.author: John Milton
examples.why: Milton's invocation, which places his Muse on Sinai.

lines: Thesiphone, thou help me for tendyte
Thise woful vers, that wepen as I wryte!
examples.title: Troilus and Criseyde · Book I
examples.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
examples.why: Chaucer invokes a Fury instead of a Muse, fit for a tale of sorrow.

terms.short: A long monorhymed poem, usually of praise, in Arabic, Persian and Ottoman poetry.
terms.long: The qasida was the great form of pre-Islamic Arabic poetry: a poem of one metre and one rhyme, perhaps fifteen to over a hundred lines, which commonly moves from the poet weeping at an abandoned campsite, through a desert journey, to boasting or praise. The famous Mu'allaqat are qasidas. Persian and Ottoman poets made the kaside chiefly a poem of praise for God, the Prophet or a ruler, with recognised parts: an opening on nature or another theme (nesib or tesbib), a transition (girizgah), the praise itself (medhiye), the poet's praise of himself (fahriye) and a closing prayer (dua). Nef'i was its Ottoman master. In the nineteenth century Namik Kemal turned the old form to new ends in his Hürriyet Kasidesi, a kaside on liberty.

lines: Görüp ahkâm-ı asrı münharif sıdk u selametten
Çekildik izzet ü ikbal ile bab-ı hükûmetten
examples.title: Hürriyet Kasidesi
examples.author: Namık Kemal
examples.why: Namik Kemal's 'Kaside on Liberty' opens with a rhyming couplet; every second line after it rhymes in -etten.

lines: Usanmaz kendini insan bilenler halka hizmetten
Mürüvvet-mend olan mazluma el çekmez ianetten
examples.title: Hürriyet Kasidesi
examples.author: Namık Kemal
examples.why: The single rhyme continues through the poem.

terms.short: A compressed poetic name for something, usually a compound: 'whale-road' for the sea.
terms.long: Old Norse and Old English poets name things obliquely: the sea is the 'whale-road' or 'swan-road', the body the 'bone-house', a sword the 'battle-light', the sun 'heaven's candle'. A kenning is a kind of tiny riddle or metaphor that asks the listener to see a familiar thing through one of its relations. In Norse skaldic verse kennings can be stacked several deep. They also helped poets meet the demands of alliteration, since a thing could be named with many different initial sounds.

lines: ofer hronrade    hyran scolde,
gomban gyldan.    þæt wæs god cyning!
examples.title: Beowulf (Old English) · Lines 1–125
examples.author: Beowulf Poet
examples.why: Hronrad, 'whale-road', the sea.

lines: who house by the whale-path, heard his mandate,
gave him gifts:  a good king he!
examples.title: Beowulf · Prelude of the Founder of the Danish House
examples.author: Beowulf Poet
examples.why: Gummere's 'whale-path' keeps the kenning in translation.

terms.short: A comic five-line poem rhyming aabba, with a bouncing anapaestic rhythm.
terms.long: Edward Lear popularised the limerick in his Book of Nonsense (1846). The first, second and fifth lines are longer, with three beats; the third and fourth shorter, with two. Lear's last line usually repeats the first with a small change; later writers preferred a punchline. Lear's nonsense is gentle and strange rather than bawdy: his old men and young ladies are often victims of their own oddities, and the illustrations he drew were part of the joke. The limerick soon became the most popular comic verse form in English, passed on by word of mouth as much as in print.

lines: There was an Old Man with a beard,
Who sat on a Horse when he reared;
examples.title: There was an Old Man with a beard
examples.author: Edward Lear
examples.why: Lear's limerick: the long first line, then the comic catastrophe.

terms.short: A ballad written by a known poet in imitation of the traditional ballads.
terms.long: Once the old ballads were in print, poets began to write their own. The literary ballad keeps the simple stanza, the swift story, the dialogue and the strangeness of its models, but it is composed on paper and often carries more symbol and more self-consciousness. Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner (1798), Keats's 'La Belle Dame sans Merci' (1819) and Wilde's Ballad of Reading Gaol (1898) are famous examples.

lines: "I met a lady in the meads,
Full beautiful--a faery's child,
examples.title: La Belle Dame Sans Merci
examples.author: John Keats
examples.why: The knight's encounter with the fairy lady, told in a ballad stanza with a shortened last line.

lines: Water, water, every where,
And all the boards did shrink;
examples.title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
examples.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
examples.why: Coleridge's ballad uses repetition as the old songs do.

terms.short: Understatement by denying the opposite: 'not bad' for 'good'.
terms.long: Litotes says less to mean more. It is a favourite figure of Old English poetry, whose grim reticence speaks of a disaster as something not pleasant, or of a hero as 'not slow'. In everyday English it survives in phrases such as 'no small achievement'. Old English verse often prefers to say less than it means, so that a hero who suffers greatly is said to have had 'no easy time', or a defeat is described as 'not a joyful outcome'. The effect can be grim, ironic or quietly emphatic, and it is part of the heroic poetry's restraint.

lines: Nor was that the meanest of mighty helps
which Hrothgar's orator offered at need:
examples.title: Beowulf · Fitt XXI
examples.author: Beowulf Poet
examples.why: The sword lent to Beowulf is praised by saying it was not the least of helps.

lines: angry and eager. That edge was not useless
to the warrior now. He wished with speed
examples.title: Beowulf · Fitt XXIII
examples.author: Beowulf Poet
examples.why: Understatement for a sword that did its work.

terms.short: A short poem expressing the thoughts or feelings of a single speaker.
terms.long: Named after the lyre that accompanied Greek song, the lyric is now the broadest kind of poem: short, personal, concentrated on a moment, a mood or a perception, rather than on telling a story (narrative) or presenting characters (drama). Sonnets, odes, songs, elegies and most short poems are lyrics. The speaker of a lyric is not always the poet; it is safer to call the voice 'the speaker'.

lines: I wandered lonely as a cloud
That floats on high o’er vales and hills,
examples.title: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
examples.author: William Wordsworth
examples.why: Wordsworth's daffodils: a single remembered moment and its feeling.

lines: Break, break, break,
On thy cold gray stones, O Sea!
examples.title: Break, Break, Break
examples.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
examples.why: Tennyson's brief lyric of grief beside the sea.

terms.short: The pen name a poet works into the last couplet of a gazel, as a signature.
terms.long: Persian, Ottoman and Urdu poets took a pen name (Persian takhallus, Turkish mahlas), and by custom used it in the closing couplet of a gazel, often addressing themselves: 'Fuzuli' (from an Arabic word for excess, or meddling), 'Baki' (lasting), 'Nedim' (boon companion). The signature couplet is where the poet steps forward to comment on the poem's feeling. Many folk poets in Turkey signed their koşmas the same way in the final stanza.

lines: Within her ward, with garments rent, on all sides rosy-cheeked ones stray;
Fuzûlî, through those radiant hues, that quarter beams a garden fair.
examples.title: Strange If Beauties' Hearts Turn Blood
examples.author: Fuzuli
examples.why: Fuzuli signs this gazel with his pen name in its last couplet.

terms.short: A long poem in rhyming couplets, each with its own rhyme, used for stories, romances and mystical teaching.
terms.long: The masnavi is the Persian narrative form: couplets rhyming aa, bb, cc, so that, unlike the gazel or kaside, it can run for thousands of lines. Firdausi's Shahnameh, Nizami's romances and Rumi's six-book Masnavi, the great poem of Sufi teaching, are masnavis. Ottoman poets took it up as the mesnevi for romances such as Fuzuli's Leyla vü Mecnun and Seyh Galib's Hüsn ü Aşk (Beauty and Love, 1783), and for moral and religious poems. English translators often used the heroic couplet to match it.

lines: A prince there was, long since in time it is.
Of Church and State the power and wealth were his.
examples.title: The Mesnevi, Book the First · Tale I: The Prince and the Handmaid
examples.author: Jalal al-Din Rumi
examples.why: Redhouse renders Rumi's Mesnevi in rhyming couplets, as the original is written.

lines: HEARKEN to the reed-flute, how it complains,
Lamenting its banishment from its home:
examples.title: The Masnavi (abridged), Books I–VI · Book I — Prologue
examples.author: Jalal al-Din Rumi
examples.why: Whinfield's abridged English Masnavi, opening with the song of the reed.

terms.short: A figure that speaks of one thing in terms of another, without 'like' or 'as'.
terms.long: In metaphor the comparison is implied: 'Hope is the thing with feathers'. Aristotle thought the command of metaphor the mark of genius, since it shows an eye for resemblances. Much ordinary language is dead metaphor. Extended metaphors run through a poem; a strained or ingenious one is a conceit; a compressed Old English one is a kenning. A metaphor has two parts, which I. A. Richards called the tenor (the subject) and the vehicle (the image it is described through). In 'Hope is the thing with feathers', hope is the tenor and the bird the vehicle. A mixed metaphor joins vehicles that do not fit together.

lines: Hope is the thing with feathers
That perches in the soul,
examples.title: Hope is the thing with feathers
examples.author: Emily Dickinson
examples.why: Dickinson makes hope a bird without saying 'like'.

lines: Bare ruin'd choirs, where late the sweet birds sang.
In me thou see'st the twilight of such day
examples.title: Sonnet 73
examples.author: William Shakespeare
examples.why: Shakespeare's bare boughs become ruined church choirs.

terms.short: The regular pattern of rhythm in verse, measured in feet, stresses, syllables or syllable lengths.
terms.long: Different languages measure verse differently. Greek and Latin (and Arabic, Persian and Ottoman aruz) count long and short syllables; French and Turkish hece count syllables; Old English counts stresses; and most English verse since Chaucer counts both stresses and syllables (accentual-syllabic metre), in feet such as the iamb. A metre is named by its foot and the number of feet: iambic pentameter, trochaic tetrameter. Poems rarely keep a metre with mechanical regularity; the interest lies in how the living rhythm plays against the pattern.

lines: Of Mans First Disobedience, and the Fruit
Of that Forbidden Tree, whose mortal tast
examples.title: Paradise Lost · Book I
examples.author: John Milton
examples.why: Ten syllables, five beats: iambic pentameter.
