On the great Red Pipe-stone Quarry,
examples.title: The Song of Hiawatha · The Peace-Pipe
examples.author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
examples.why: Longfellow's trochaic tetrameter, a strongly marked metre.

terms.short: A poem that treats a trivial subject in the grand style of epic, for comic or satirical effect.
terms.long: The mock-epic borrows everything the epic has (invocations, battles, gods, catalogues, a journey to the underworld) and applies it to something small: a stolen lock of hair, a quarrel over a bucket, a city's dull poets. The gap between style and subject makes the joke, and lets the poet satirise the present by holding it against the heroic past. Pope's The Rape of the Lock (1714) is the masterpiece; Dryden's Mac Flecknoe and Pope's own Dunciad turn the method into literary satire.

lines: What dire offence from amorous causes springs,
What mighty contests rise from trivial things,
examples.title: The Rape of the Lock
examples.author: Alexander Pope
examples.why: Pope's epic opening for a poem about the theft of a curl.

lines: Or stain her honour, or her new brocade;
Forget her prayers, or miss a masquerade;
examples.title: The Rape of the Lock
examples.author: Alexander Pope
examples.why: A line that weighs a lady's honour and her new dress equally.

terms.short: A poem that tells a story, with characters, events and usually a narrator.
terms.long: Alongside lyric and drama, narrative is one of the three broad kinds of poetry. Epics, romances, ballads, verse tales and verse novels are all narrative poems, from Homer to Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, Scott's verse romances, Longfellow's Evangeline and Elizabeth Barrett Browning's Aurora Leigh. A narrative poem has a teller, who may be the poet or a character, and can range from the impersonal ballad to the chatty, digressive narrator of Byron's Don Juan.

lines: WHEN that Aprilis, with his showers swoot,
The drought of March hath pierced to the root,
examples.title: The Canterbury Tales · The General Prologue
examples.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
examples.why: The opening of the Canterbury Tales, setting the season for a pilgrimage.

lines: In the Acadian land, on the shores of the Basin of Minas,
Distant, secluded, still, the little village of Grand-Pre
examples.title: Evangeline · Part the First, I
examples.author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
examples.why: Longfellow's Evangeline, a story told in hexameters.

terms.short: A unit of eight lines, especially the first eight lines of a Petrarchan sonnet.
terms.long: In the Italian sonnet the octave is the first part of the poem, rhyming abbaabba, where the subject or problem is stated before the volta. The word is also used for any eight-line stanza, such as ottava rima. Because the octave's two rhymes each sound four times, it tends to feel enclosed and complete, and the sestet that follows can feel like release.

lines: Much have I traveled in the realms of gold,
And many goodly states and kingdoms seen;
examples.title: On First Looking into Chapman's Homer
examples.author: John Keats
examples.why: The first two lines of Keats's octave, which uses only two rhymes, on -old and -een.

terms.short: A long lyric poem of address, serious in tone and elaborate in stanza.
terms.long: The ode descends from Greek songs performed in public: Pindar's odes for athletic victors, sung by a chorus, and the more personal odes of Horace in Latin. English poets made three kinds. The Pindaric ode has a pattern of strophe, antistrophe and epode; the Horatian ode repeats one stanza throughout; the irregular ode, popularised by Cowley, lets each stanza find its own shape. An ode usually addresses someone or something (a nightingale, the West Wind, Duty, Evening) and moves from description to meditation. The great Romantic odes of Keats, Shelley and Wordsworth made the form the place for a poet's most searching thought.

lines: Thou still unravish’d bride of quietness,
Thou foster-child of silence and slow time,
examples.title: Ode on a Grecian Urn
examples.author: John Keats
examples.why: Keats's ode begins by addressing the Grecian urn directly.

lines: My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains
My sense, as though of hemlock I had drunk,
examples.title: Ode to a Nightingale
examples.author: John Keats
examples.why: The 'Ode to a Nightingale' opens with the speaker's own state of mind.

lines: If aught of oaten stop, or pastoral song,
May hope, chaste Eve, to soothe thy modest ear,
examples.title: Ode to Evening
examples.author: William Collins
examples.why: Collins addresses Evening in an unrhymed ode.

terms.short: Words that imitate the sounds they describe.
terms.long: 'Buzz', 'murmur', 'hiss'. Poets use such words, and the sounds of language more broadly, to echo their subject: Poe's 'The Bells' makes its words tinkle, clang and toll; Tennyson's 'murmuring of innumerable bees' hums. Few words are purely imitative, and different languages imitate the same sound differently, so onomatopoeia is partly a matter of convention. In poetry the term is often used more widely for any matching of sound to sense, as when Pope makes a line move slowly to describe a slow movement.

lines: Hear the sledges with the bells--
Silver bells!
examples.title: The Bells
examples.author: Edgar Allan Poe
examples.why: Poe's 'The Bells', which imitates sleigh-bells, wedding bells, alarm bells and funeral bells.

terms.short: An eight-line stanza rhyming abababcc, used by Italian romance poets and by Byron.
terms.long: Boccaccio, Ariosto and Tasso told their long stories in ottava rima, and English translators such as Harington (Ariosto) and Fairfax (Tasso) followed them. Its six alternating rhymes build up, and the final couplet can clinch or deflate. Byron found the deflating possibility irresistible: in Beppo and Don Juan the couplet repeatedly punctures the stanza's own seriousness, often with a comic rhyme.

lines: I want a hero: an uncommon want,
When every year and month sends forth a new one,
examples.title: Don Juan · Canto I
examples.author: Lord Byron
examples.why: Byron's first stanza: six alternating rhymes and a closing couplet.

lines: God sends his angel to Tortosa down,
Godfrey unites the Christian Peers and Knights;
examples.title: Jerusalem Delivered · Book I
examples.author: Torquato Tasso
examples.why: Fairfax's Tasso, in ottava rima like the Italian.

lines: Fair Isabel, poor simple Isabel!
Lorenzo, a young palmer in Love's eye!
examples.title: Isabella; or, The Pot of Basil
examples.author: John Keats
examples.why: Keats's 'Isabella', a tale from Boccaccio in Boccaccio's stanza.

terms.short: Poetry of shepherds and country life, imagined as simple, idle and in harmony with nature.
terms.long: Theocritus wrote the first pastorals in Sicily in the third century BC, and Virgil's Eclogues made the shepherd's world a place for poems about love, poetry and politics. The pastoral is not realistic farming poetry: its shepherds sing, compete in verse and mourn their dead in an idealised landscape. Renaissance poets loved it: Spenser's The Shepheardes Calender (1579), Marlowe's 'Passionate Shepherd'. The pastoral elegy is one of its branches; the georgic, on actual farm work, is its working cousin.

lines: Come live with me and be my love,
And we will all the pleasures prove
examples.title: The Passionate Shepherd to His Love
examples.author: Christopher Marlowe
examples.why: Marlowe's shepherd invites his love to an idyll of pleasures.

lines: Together both, ere the high Lawns appear'd
Under the opening eye-lids of the morn,
examples.title: Lycidas
examples.author: John Milton
examples.why: In Lycidas, Milton remembers student friendship as shepherds tending flocks.

terms.short: An elegy in which the poet and the dead are imagined as shepherds, with a set series of conventions.
terms.long: The form goes back to Theocritus, Bion and Virgil. Its conventions are strong: the dead is a shepherd-poet; the speaker calls on the Muses; nature mourns; a procession of mourners passes; the speaker asks where the guardian spirits were; flowers are strewn; and finally grief turns to consolation, often with the claim that the dead lives on. Milton's Lycidas (1638) for Edward King, Shelley's Adonais (1821) for Keats and Arnold's Thyrsis (1866) for Clough are the great English examples.

lines: YET once more, O ye Laurels, and once more
Ye Myrtles brown, with Ivy never-sear,
examples.title: Lycidas
examples.author: John Milton
examples.why: Lycidas opens as the shepherd-poet plucks unripe berries for the dead.

lines: I weep for Adonais—he is dead!
O, weep for Adonais! though our tears
examples.title: Adonais
examples.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
examples.why: Shelley's elegy for Keats begins by naming the dead with a pastoral name.

lines: How changed is here each spot man makes or fills!
In the two Hinkseys nothing keeps the same;
examples.title: Thyrsis
examples.author: Matthew Arnold
examples.why: Arnold returns to the Oxford countryside he and Clough walked.

terms.short: Attributing human feelings to nature, as when the weather seems to share a mood.
terms.long: John Ruskin coined the phrase in Modern Painters (1856), mildly disapproving of the 'false appearances' that strong feeling gives to things, such as a 'cruel' foam. The term is now used neutrally. Pastoral elegy depends on it: in Lycidas the willows and hazel copses mourn the dead. Ruskin used the phrase to criticise what he saw as sentimental distortion, but poets have always found it a powerful way to show emotion. In the elegy, nature's mourning makes the loss seem universal; in other poems, a storm or a calm can mirror a character's state of mind.

lines: The Willows, and the Hazle Copses green,
Shall now no more be seen,
examples.title: Lycidas
examples.author: John Milton
examples.why: In Lycidas, the trees no longer fan their leaves for the dead poet.

lines: Break, break, break,
On thy cold gray stones, O Sea!
examples.title: Break, Break, Break
examples.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
examples.why: Tennyson's sea seems to beat with his grief.

terms.short: A line of five metrical feet.
terms.long: In English, pentameter almost always means iambic pentameter. In classical prosody the 'pentameter' is the second line of the elegiac couplet, made of two halves of two and a half dactylic feet each. The word means 'five measures'. Ten-syllable lines in English are almost always heard as five beats, and pentameter has been the dominant line of English verse for six centuries, used for sonnets, plays, epics and verse letters. Lines of four beats (tetrameter) and of six (hexameter) are its nearest neighbours.

lines: In the pentameter aye falling in melody back.
examples.title: The Ovidian Elegiac Metre Described and Exemplified
examples.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
examples.why: Coleridge's line imitates the classical pentameter falling back.

terms.short: Giving human qualities or a human form to something not human, such as an idea, a season or a thing.
terms.long: Personified figures (Death, Time, Fortune, Melancholy) fill medieval allegory and eighteenth-century odes. Keats's 'To Autumn' personifies the season as a figure sitting careless on a granary floor or asleep in a half-reaped furrow. When a personified thing is addressed directly, personification combines with apostrophe. Personification ranges from a capital letter on an abstract noun to a fully imagined character with a body, a voice and a story. Medieval morality plays and allegories gave Death, Vice and Good Deeds their own parts; eighteenth-century odes filled their stanzas with Fear, Pity and Melancholy.

lines: Who hath not seen thee oft amid thy store?
Sometimes whoever seeks abroad may find
examples.title: To Autumn
examples.author: John Keats
examples.why: Keats imagines Autumn as a person to be found about the farm.

lines: Death be not proud, though some have called thee
Mighty and dreadfull, for, thou art not soe,
examples.title: (untitled)
examples.author: John Donne
examples.why: Donne addresses Death as a person, and a proud one.

terms.short: A sonnet of an octave rhyming abbaabba and a sestet on two or three new rhymes, with the turn between them.
terms.long: Named after Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch), whose Italian love sonnets were the model for Renaissance Europe, this sonnet is built in two unequal parts. The octave, the first eight lines, uses only two rhymes in the pattern abbaabba and presents a situation or a feeling. The sestet, the last six, brings new rhymes (cdecde, cdcdcd and other arrangements) and answers, qualifies or reverses it. The change at line nine is the volta. Because English has fewer rhymes than Italian, the four-fold rhymes of the octave are a real test, and Milton, Wordsworth and Keats valued the form for that discipline. Milton sometimes let his sense run past the break; Wordsworth called the sonnet's narrow room a welcome confinement.

lines: When I consider how my light is spent,
Ere half my days, in this dark world and wide,
examples.title: Sonnet 19: When I Consider How My Light Is Spent
examples.author: John Milton
examples.why: Milton's octave sets out the complaint of a blind poet who fears his talent is wasted.

lines: I fondly ask. But patience, to prevent
That murmur, soon replies, “God doth not need
examples.title: Sonnet 19: When I Consider How My Light Is Spent
examples.author: John Milton
examples.why: The volta: Patience interrupts at the end of line eight and answers in the sestet.

lines: Then felt I like some watcher of the skies
When a new planet swims into his ken;
examples.title: On First Looking into Chapman's Homer
examples.author: John Keats
examples.why: Keats's sestet turns from report to wonder, with the image of an astronomer finding a planet.

terms.short: An ode on the model of Pindar, in groups of strophe, antistrophe and epode, or in loose irregular stanzas.
terms.long: Pindar (c. 518-438 BC) wrote choral odes for victors at the Greek games. Each was built in triads: a strophe, an antistrophe in exactly the same metre, and an epode in a different one. Cowley's Pindarique Odes (1656) misread Pindar as metrically free, and for a century the 'Pindaric' meant a poem of lofty enthusiasm in stanzas of varying length. Gray's 'The Progress of Poesy' and 'The Bard' restored the true triadic pattern, while Dryden's odes for St Cecilia's Day and Wordsworth's 'Intimations of Immortality' follow the irregular kind.

lines: Awake, Æolian lyre, awake,
And give to rapture all thy trembling strings.
examples.title: The Progress of Poesy: A Pindaric Ode
examples.author: Thomas Gray
examples.why: Gray's Pindaric ode on poetry opens its first strophe with an invocation of the lyre.

lines: 'Twas at the royal feast, for Persia won
By Philip's warlike son:
examples.title: Alexander's Feast; or, The Power of Music
examples.author: John Dryden
examples.why: Dryden's irregular ode for St Cecilia's Day, with stanzas of different lengths.

lines: There was a time when meadow, grove, and stream,
The earth, and every common sight,
examples.title: Ode: Intimations of Immortality
examples.author: William Wordsworth
examples.why: Wordsworth's great irregular ode begins with the loss of a child's vision.

terms.short: Metre based on the length (quantity) of syllables, not on stress, as in Greek, Latin and Arabic verse.
terms.long: Greek and Latin verse arranged long and short syllables in fixed patterns; a syllable was long if it had a long vowel or ended in a consonant before another. Arabic, Persian and Ottoman aruz is also quantitative. English, a stress language, cannot really hear length, and Elizabethan experiments in 'classical' English quantitative verse (Sidney, Campion, Stanyhurst's Aeneid) remained curiosities; later imitations such as Coleridge's and Longfellow's substitute stress for length.

lines: So spake the voice: and as with a single life
Instinct, the whole mass, fierce, irretainable,
examples.title: Alcaics
examples.author: Arthur Hugh Clough
examples.why: Clough's 'Alcaics', an English poem in a Greek stanza.

lines: I That in old season wyth reeds oten harmonye whistled
My rural sonnet; from forrest flitted (I) forced
examples.title: The First Four Books of the Aeneid (Stanyhurst) · Book I
examples.author: Virgil
examples.why: Stanyhurst's Aeneid (1582), a famous Elizabethan attempt at English hexameters.

terms.short: A stanza of four lines, the most common stanza in English.
terms.long: Quatrains may rhyme abab (the heroic or elegiac quatrain of Gray's Elegy), abcb (the ballad stanza), abba (Tennyson's In Memoriam stanza) or aaba (the rubai). The Shakespearean sonnet is built of three quatrains and a couplet. The quatrain is long enough for a complete sentence and short enough to stay memorable. Because it is so common, the quatrain is the stanza against which other forms are felt. A poet can make it march, as in hymns and ballads, or slow it down with long lines and enclosed rhymes, as in Gray's Elegy and Tennyson's In Memoriam.

lines: The curfew tolls the knell of parting day,
The lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea,
examples.title: Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard
examples.author: Thomas Gray
examples.why: Gray's elegiac quatrain, pentameter rhyming abab.

lines: I wandered through each chartered street,
Near where the chartered Thames does flow,
examples.title: London
examples.author: William Blake
examples.why: Blake's 'London' in tetrameter quatrains.

terms.short: In the gazel and kaside, a word or phrase repeated after the rhyme at the end of every rhyming line.
terms.long: In Persian and Ottoman poetry a line's rhyme (kafiye) may be followed by a redif, a word or a few words that recur unchanged, so that the rhyme sounds just before it. In a gazel with the redif 'in mystic dance' the rhymes might be 'here', 'sphere', 'appear' with the same phrase after each. The redif gives the poem a refrain-like insistence while the rhymes before it keep changing. It is a mark of skill to find a redif that can be met freshly every time.

lines: Sun and moon traverse the sphere in mystic dance.
Love's deep secret made the spheric heavens reel;
examples.title: While the Lovers Circle Here in Mystic Dance
examples.author: Şeyh Galip
examples.why: The redif 'in mystic dance' follows the rhyme in every second line.

lines: Faith, idol, Ka'ba-fane am I; who smites the sphere a-spin am I;
The cloud upon the heavens' face, likewise the rains that rain am I.
examples.title: Faith, Idol, Ka'ba-Fane Am I
examples.author: Yunus Emre
examples.why: Yunus Emre's lines end on the same 'am I', as the redif does in his Turkish.

terms.short: A line or group of lines repeated at intervals, especially at the ends of stanzas.
terms.long: Refrains come from song: the chorus everyone joins in. In ballads, the refrain may be nonsense syllables or a repeated line; in the villanelle, rondeau and ballade, it is a formal requirement. A good refrain gathers new meaning as the poem changes around it, as in Tennyson's 'Mariana' ('He cometh not, she said') or Spenser's Epithalamion. A refrain can be a whole stanza, a single line, a phrase or even a single word. It can stay exactly the same, so that its meaning shifts around it, or change slightly each time, as in Spenser's Epithalamion, where the woods first answer and finally fall silent. Many refrains invite listeners to join in.

lines: He cometh not," she said;
She said "I am aweary, aweary;
examples.title: Mariana
examples.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
examples.why: The refrain of Mariana's hopeless waiting.

lines: The woods shall to me answer, and my Eccho ring.
Early, before the worlds light-giving lampe
examples.title: Epithalamion
examples.author: Edmund Spenser
examples.why: Spenser's wedding refrain.

terms.short: The matching of sounds at the ends of words, from the last stressed vowel on.
terms.long: Full rhyme pairs words whose final stressed vowel and everything after it sound the same (day/away; painted/acquainted). Rhyme was unknown in classical verse; it entered European poetry through medieval Latin hymns and became the norm in English after the Norman Conquest. A rhyme scheme is written with letters (abab). Variants include slant rhyme, internal rhyme and eye rhyme (love/move, which match only on the page).

lines: Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
examples.title: Sonnet 18
examples.author: William Shakespeare
examples.why: The first rhymes of Sonnet 18: day and temperate, set up to be answered by May and date.

lines: True ease in writing comes from art, not chance,
As those move easiest who have learn'd to dance.
examples.title: An Essay on Criticism
examples.author: Alexander Pope
examples.why: Pope's rhymes clinch his couplets.

terms.short: A seven-line stanza of iambic pentameter rhyming ababbcc.
terms.long: Chaucer introduced the stanza in Troilus and Criseyde and the Parliament of Fowls; the name is said to come from its use by King James I of Scotland in The Kingis Quair. Its third and fourth lines rhyme together in the middle, and the closing couplet gives each stanza a firm end without the snap of a single couplet poem. It was the stanza of serious narrative before Spenser: Shakespeare's The Rape of Lucrece and Wyatt's 'They flee from me' use it.

lines: The double sorwe of Troilus to tellen,
That was the king Priamus sone of Troye,
examples.title: Troilus and Criseyde · Book I
examples.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
examples.why: Chaucer opens Troilus in rhyme royal: tellen, Troye, fellen, Ioye, ye, tendyte, wryte.

lines: They flee from me that sometime did me seek,
With naked foot stalking within my chamber:
examples.title: They Flee from Me
examples.author: Sir Thomas Wyatt
examples.why: Wyatt's poem of lost favour, in three stanzas of rhyme royal.

terms.short: A poem that describes something indirectly and asks the reader to name it.
terms.long: Riddles are among the oldest kinds of poem. The Exeter Book, copied in England in the late tenth century, holds about ninety-five Old English verse riddles, in which an object often speaks for itself ('I am...') and ends with a challenge to 'say what I am called'. Their answers (a bookworm, a shield, a storm, an onion) are not given in the manuscript, and some are still disputed. Riddles teach a way of looking: they make the ordinary strange.

lines: A moth ate a word. To me that seemed
A curious happening when I heard of that wonder,
examples.title: Riddle XLVII. A Bookworm
examples.author: Anonymous (Old English)
examples.why: The bookworm riddle, about a moth that eats words without growing wiser.
examples.translator: trans. Cosette Faust Newton & Stith Thompson (1918)

lines: Moððe word fræt.    Me þæt þuhte
wrætlicu wyrd,    þa ic þæt wundor gefrægn,
examples.title: Riddle 47 (Old English)
examples.author: Anonymous (Old English)
examples.why: The same riddle in Old English.

terms.short: A tale of knights, love, quests and marvels, the chief narrative form of the Middle Ages.
terms.long: Medieval romances, first in French and then in English, tell of knights who ride out on quests, face giants and enchantments, and are tested in courage and courtesy, often for a lady's sake. The matter of Britain (Arthur and his court), of France (Charlemagne) and of Rome (Troy, Alexander) supplied the stories. English romances such as Sir Orfeo, Havelok and Sir Gawain and the Green Knight were in rhymed couplets, tail-rhyme stanzas or alliterative verse. Spenser's Faerie Queene is a Renaissance romance-epic.

lines: Siþen þe sege & þe assaut watȝ sesed at Troye,
Þe borȝ brittened & brent to brondeȝ & askeȝ,
examples.title: Sir Gawayne and the Grene Knyȝt (Middle English text) · Fitt I
examples.author: Gawain Poet
examples.why: Sir Gawain begins by tracing Britain's founding back to the fall of Troy.

lines: We redyn ofte, and fynde ywryte,
As clerkes don us to wyte,
examples.title: Sir Orpheo · Lines 1–256
examples.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
examples.why: Sir Orfeo retells the Orpheus story as a Breton lay of a king who wins his queen back from fairyland.

terms.short: A French form of fifteen lines on two rhymes, with the opening words returning twice as a short refrain.
terms.long: The rondeau comes from medieval French song. In its usual later form it has thirteen full lines on two rhymes, in three stanzas (five, three and five lines), and the first words of the poem return, unrhymed, after the second and third stanzas, making fifteen lines. The refrain gains new meaning each time. Wyatt wrote rondeaus in the sixteenth century; Victorian poets such as Dobson, Henley and Dowson revived them. John McCrae's 'In Flanders Fields' (1915) is a rondeau.

lines: In Flanders fields the poppies blow
Between the crosses, row on row,
examples.title: In Flanders Fields
examples.author: John McCrae
examples.why: The opening words, 'In Flanders fields', return as the poem's refrain.

lines: Ah, Manon, say, why is it we
Are one and all so fain of thee?
examples.title: Rondeau
examples.author: Ernest Dowson
examples.why: A rondeau by Ernest Dowson.

terms.short: A Persian quatrain, rhyming aaba or aaaa, complete in itself.
terms.long: The rubai (plural rubaiyat) is a four-line poem in a set metre, rhyming on the first, second and fourth lines (sometimes all four). Its third line, unrhymed, often holds back the point for the last. Omar Khayyam (1048-1131) is the poet the form is most associated with, though many quatrains attributed to him are probably by others. Edward FitzGerald's free English Rubaiyat (1859) kept the aaba pattern and made the stanza famous in English; Ottoman poets also wrote rubais.

lines: Here with a Loaf of Bread beneath the Bough,
A Flask of Wine, a Book of Verse--and Thou
examples.title: The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam · XI
examples.author: Edward FitzGerald
examples.why: One of FitzGerald's quatrains, with its unrhymed third line.
examples.translator: trans. Edward FitzGerald (1859), from Omar Khayyam

lines: Awake! for Morning in the Bowl of Night
Has flung the Stone that puts the Stars to Flight:
examples.title: The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam · I
examples.author: Edward FitzGerald
examples.why: The first quatrain of FitzGerald's 1859 version.
examples.translator: trans. Edward FitzGerald (1859), from Omar Khayyam

terms.short: A Greek lyric stanza of three eleven-syllable lines and a short fifth-syllable line, named after Sappho.
terms.long: Sappho of Lesbos used the stanza for her lyrics, and Catullus and Horace took it into Latin. Its short fourth line (an adonic, DUM-de-de-DUM-de) closes each stanza with a falling cadence. Swinburne and others wrote English sapphics by stress. Sappho's poems survive mostly in fragments, quoted by later writers or found on papyrus, and the stanza named after her is one of the best-known parts of her legacy. In English, the form has been used by Isaac Watts, Cowper, Swinburne and Hardy, among others, usually with stress standing in for length.

lines: Love, like an island, held a single heart,
Waiting for shoreward flutterings of the breeze,
examples.title: Sapphics
examples.author: William Johnson Cory
examples.why: William Johnson Cory's English sapphics.

lines: Clothed in splendour, beautifully sad and silent,
Comes the autumn over the woods and highlands,
examples.title: Sapphics
examples.author: Archibald Lampman
examples.why: Archibald Lampman's 'Sapphics'.

terms.short: Writing that mocks vice and folly, to amuse and to correct.
terms.long: Roman satire took two forms: the genial, conversational kind of Horace and the furious kind of Juvenal. English verse satire flourished from the 1590s and reached its height with Dryden, Pope and Swift, whose heroic couplets could cut a reputation in two lines. Satire uses irony, caricature, parody and the mock-heroic. Byron's Don Juan carried it into the nineteenth century in ottava rima.

lines: All human things are subject to decay,
And when fate summons, monarchs must obey.
examples.title: Mac Flecknoe
examples.author: John Dryden
examples.why: Dryden's Mac Flecknoe opens with a grave reflection that sets up a comic coronation of a bad poet.

lines: I want a hero: an uncommon want,
When every year and month sends forth a new one,
examples.title: Don Juan · Canto I
examples.author: Lord Byron
examples.why: Byron's satirical epic begins by mocking the search for a hero.

terms.short: Marking a line's stressed and unstressed syllables to show its metre.
terms.long: To scan a line is to read it for its rhythm and mark where the stresses fall, then divide it into feet. Scansion shows both the pattern and the poet's variations: an inverted first foot, a spondee, a missing syllable. Readers do not always agree, because English stress is a matter of degree and of interpretation. Readers usually mark stressed syllables with a stroke (/) and unstressed ones with a cross (x) or a curved mark, and divide the feet with vertical lines. Scansion is a tool for listening, not an end in itself: its value lies in noticing where the rhythm reinforces or strains against what the words say.

lines: HALF a league, half a league,
Half a league onward,
examples.title: The Charge of the Light Brigade
examples.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
examples.why: A line that scans easily as dactyls.

terms.short: A unit of six lines, especially the last six lines of a Petrarchan sonnet.
terms.long: The sestet follows the volta in an Italian sonnet and brings two or three new rhymes, arranged in many ways (cdecde, cdcdcd, cdedce). It usually answers, applies or reverses what the octave set out. The term is also used for any six-line stanza; the sestina is built of six of them. Where the octave states, the sestet often applies, answers or turns away, so the weight of a sonnet's meaning tends to fall here. Milton and Wordsworth sometimes began the sestet a little before line nine, and the English sonnet has no separate sestet at all, only a third quatrain and a couplet.

lines: They also serve who only stand and wait.”
examples.title: Sonnet 19: When I Consider How My Light Is Spent
examples.author: John Milton
examples.why: The last line of Milton's sestet gives the poem's answer in a single sentence.

lines: Then felt I like some watcher of the skies
When a new planet swims into his ken;
examples.title: On First Looking into Chapman's Homer
examples.author: John Keats
examples.why: The start of Keats's sestet, where the reading of Homer becomes a discovery.

terms.short: A poem of six six-line stanzas that reuse the same six end-words in a rotating order, closed by a three-line envoi.
terms.long: Invented by the Provençal troubadour Arnaut Daniel in the twelfth century and used by Dante and Petrarch, the sestina does without rhyme. Instead, the six words that end the lines of the first stanza end the lines of every stanza, in a fixed shuffled order (the last word of each stanza becomes the first of the next), and all six appear in the envoi. The form circles its themes and suits obsession. Sidney's double sestina 'Ye goatherd gods' and Swinburne's and Kipling's sestinas are examples.

lines: Speakin' in general, I 'ave tried 'em all,
The 'appy roads that take you o'er the world.
examples.title: Sestina of the Tramp-Royal
examples.author: Rudyard Kipling
examples.why: Kipling's 'Sestina of the Tramp-Royal' gives a wanderer's voice to the strict form.

lines: I saw my soul at rest upon a day
As a bird sleeping in the nest of night,
examples.title: Sestina
examples.author: Algernon Charles Swinburne
examples.why: Swinburne's sestina.

terms.short: A sonnet of three quatrains and a couplet, rhyming abab cdcd efef gg.
terms.long: The English sonnet was shaped by Surrey in the 1540s and is named after Shakespeare, whose 154 sonnets (printed in 1609) are its best-known examples. It uses seven rhymes instead of the Italian sonnet's four or five, which suits a language poorer in rhymes. Each of the three quatrains often develops one image or step of an argument, and the closing couplet sums up, twists or undercuts what came before. The turn may come at line nine, as in the Italian form, but the couplet always has the last word, and readers have long debated whether Shakespeare's couplets resolve his poems or merely close them.

lines: That time of year thou mayst in me behold
When yellow leaves, or none, or few, do hang
examples.title: Sonnet 73
examples.author: William Shakespeare
examples.why: The first of Sonnet 73's three quatrains, each a new image of ageing (autumn, twilight, a dying fire).

lines: This thou perceiv'st, which makes thy love more strong,
To love that well, which thou must leave ere long.
examples.title: Sonnet 73
examples.author: William Shakespeare
examples.why: The couplet turns the three images into a demand on the listener.

lines: My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun;
Coral is far more red, than her lips red:
examples.title: Sonnet 130
examples.author: William Shakespeare
examples.why: Sonnet 130 opens by refusing the usual comparisons of a lady's beauty.

terms.short: A comparison of two different things using 'like' or 'as'.
terms.long: A simile states its comparison openly: 'My love is like a red, red rose'. Because it announces itself, it keeps the two things apart even as it joins them; a metaphor fuses them. Similes range from a single word to the epic simile of many lines. Similes are often thought plainer than metaphors, but they can be surprising, comic or haunting. Because the comparison is stated, a simile can be extended, qualified or even withdrawn, and some of the most memorable similes in poetry are those that seem at first to fit badly and then reveal an unexpected likeness.

lines: O my Luve’s like a red, red rose,
That’s newly sprung in June:
examples.title: A Red, Red Rose
examples.author: Robert Burns
examples.why: Burns's love is like a red, red rose, and like a melody.

lines: I wandered lonely as a cloud
That floats on high o’er vales and hills,
examples.title: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
examples.author: William Wordsworth
examples.why: Wordsworth compares himself to a cloud.

terms.short: An imperfect rhyme in which the sounds are similar but not identical.
terms.long: Slant rhymes match consonants but not vowels (love/leave), or vowels but not consonants. Older poets used them through necessity or changes in pronunciation; Emily Dickinson made them a deliberate effect, unsettling her hymn-like quatrains, and Wilfred Owen used consonantal half-rhyme in his war poems. Slant rhyme can sound accidental in a poem that otherwise rhymes fully, but used consistently it creates a feeling of something not quite resolved, which suits doubt, grief and irony. Many modern poets prefer it to full rhyme because it seems less predictable and lets them choose the most exact word rather than the most convenient.

lines: Since then 't is centuries; but each
Feels shorter than the day
I first surmised the horses' heads
Were toward eternity.
examples.title: Because I could not stop for Death
examples.author: Emily Dickinson
examples.why: Day and eternity: Dickinson's last stanza closes on a rhyme that only half chimes.

lines: The eyes beside had wrung them dry,
And breaths were gathering sure
For that last onset, when the king
Be witnessed in his power.
examples.title: I heard a fly buzz when I died
examples.author: Emily Dickinson
examples.why: Sure and power: a slant rhyme where the hymn tune expects a full one.

terms.short: A poem written to be sung, or written in the manner of one: short, musical and stanzaic.
terms.long: Much early lyric poetry was written for music: Elizabethan songs for the lute, songs in plays, Burns's songs set to Scottish airs. A song favours regular stanzas, simple syntax, repetition and refrain, and a single feeling. Many poems called 'Song' were never set, but keep the form's lightness. The Codex marks a poem as a song when its title calls it one.

lines: O my Luve’s like a red, red rose,
That’s newly sprung in June:
examples.title: A Red, Red Rose
examples.author: Robert Burns
examples.why: Burns wrote 'A Red, Red Rose' to an old Scots tune.

lines: DRINK to me only with thine eyes,
And I will pledge with mine;
examples.title: To Celia
examples.author: Ben Jonson
examples.why: Jonson's 'To Celia', later sung to a famous eighteenth-century tune.

terms.short: A poem of fourteen lines, usually in iambic pentameter, with a set pattern of rhyme and a turn in its thought.
terms.long: The sonnet came into English from Italy in the sixteenth century, when Wyatt and Surrey imitated Petrarch, and it has never left. Its fourteen lines are long enough to state a problem and short enough to force a decision about it, which is why so many sonnets argue with themselves: a situation is set out, then turned, questioned or answered. English poets use two main shapes. The Italian or Petrarchan sonnet divides into eight lines and six; the English or Shakespearean sonnet runs three quatrains and a closing couplet. Spenser's variant links its quatrains by rhyme. Sonnets were written singly, as occasional poems on public events, and in long sequences that tell the story of a love. The Codex marks a poem as a sonnet when its title says so or when it has the form's shape.

lines: Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
examples.title: Sonnet 18
examples.author: William Shakespeare
examples.why: The question that opens Shakespeare's best-known sonnet, set in its first quatrain.

lines: Earth has not any thing to show more fair:
Dull would he be of soul who could pass by
examples.title: Composed upon Westminster Bridge, September 3, 1802
examples.author: William Wordsworth
examples.why: Wordsworth's Petrarchan sonnet on London at dawn begins with a large claim it will spend fourteen lines proving.

examples.why: Keats's sonnet on reading Homer in Chapman's translation opens its octave with a traveller's boast.

terms.short: A series of sonnets read together, often tracing the course of a love affair.
terms.long: Petrarch's sonnets to Laura became the pattern for a book of sonnets that tells, loosely, a story: the first sight of the beloved, longing, refusal, absence, sometimes death. The Elizabethans took this up in a burst in the 1590s, after Sidney's Astrophel and Stella was printed in 1591: Spenser's Amoretti, Daniel's Delia, Drayton's Idea, Shakespeare's Sonnets. The Victorians revived it, most famously in Elizabeth Barrett Browning's Sonnets from the Portuguese and Christina Rossetti's Monna Innominata. A sequence lets a poet show a feeling changing over time, and lets single sonnets answer one another.

lines: LOuing in trueth, and fayne my loue in verse to show,
That the deere Shee, might take some pleasure of my paine:
examples.title: Sonnet 1
examples.author: Sir Philip Sidney
examples.why: The first sonnet of Astrophel and Stella sets out the poet's search for words to win his lady.

But came the waves and washed it away:
examples.title: Amoretti: Sonnet LXXV
examples.author: Edmund Spenser

terms.short: The voice that speaks a poem, which need not be the poet's own.
terms.long: Readers distinguish the poet (the historical person) from the speaker (the voice the poem creates). In a dramatic monologue the speaker is plainly a character; in a lyric the speaker may be close to the poet or a mask. Calling the voice 'the speaker' avoids assuming that a poem records the poet's own experience. In older criticism the speaker was often simply identified with the poet, but most modern readers prefer to keep the two apart, especially when a poem's voice is ironic or dramatic. The distinction is useful even for personal lyrics, since a poem shapes and selects its voice.

terms.short: A sonnet of three interlocking quatrains and a couplet, rhyming abab bcbc cdcd ee.
terms.long: Edmund Spenser used this variant in Amoretti (1595), the sequence of 89 sonnets written for his courtship and marriage of Elizabeth Boyle. Like the English sonnet it has three quatrains and a couplet, but each quatrain picks up the last rhyme of the one before, so that the poem is chained together and reads with something of the Italian sonnet's continuity. Few later poets used the pattern, which needs as many matching rhymes as the Petrarchan octave.

terms.short: A nine-line stanza of eight pentameters and a closing alexandrine, rhyming ababbcbcc.
terms.long: Spenser devised this stanza for The Faerie Queene (1590-96). Its interlaced rhymes give it a slow, weaving movement, and the long final line of twelve syllables (an alexandrine) lets each stanza settle before the next. The Romantics revived it: Byron's Childe Harold, Keats's The Eve of St Agnes and Shelley's Adonais are in Spenserians. The rhyme scheme (ababbcbcc) uses only three rhymes across nine lines, so the stanza is closely woven, and the couplet that ends it is softened by the longer final line. Readers often describe its movement as leisurely and dreamlike, well suited to Spenser's slow-unfolding allegory and to Keats's richly detailed scenes.

terms.short: A metrical foot of two stressed syllables: DUM-DUM.
terms.long: In English the spondee mostly appears as a substitution for another foot, to slow a line or make it heavy ('Rocks, caves, lakes, fens, bogs, dens and shades of death', in Paradise Lost). Tennyson's 'Break, break, break' opens with stresses massed together. Some prosodists doubt that English has true spondees, since two adjacent syllables rarely carry exactly equal stress; but the term is useful for those moments when stresses crowd together and the voice slows. Such heavy feet usually stand out against a lighter pattern, so they are often used for weight, effort or finality.

terms.short: A group of lines forming a unit in a poem, usually repeated in pattern; the 'room' of a poem.
terms.long: Stanza is Italian for 'room' or 'stopping-place'. A stanza form is defined by its number of lines, their lengths and its rhyme scheme: the couplet, tercet, quatrain, rhyme royal, ottava rima, the Spenserian. Poems in blank verse or free verse divide instead into verse paragraphs of varying length. The Codex prints stanza breaks as they stand in the source edition.

examples.author: John Keats

terms.short: Verse measured by the number of syllables in a line, regardless of stress.
terms.long: French, Italian, Spanish, Japanese and Turkish folk verse (hece) are syllabic: a line has a fixed count of syllables, with stress free or fixed by the language. In English, syllabic verse is a modern experiment; most English verse counts stresses as well as syllables. In a language with weak or fixed word stress, such as French or Turkish, counting syllables gives a clear sense of measure; in English, which stresses strongly and unevenly, two lines of the same syllable count can sound very different. Marianne Moore and others in the twentieth century made syllabic English verse a deliberate art.

Gidiyorduk: İri buzlar sarkıtmıştı her saçak;

terms.short: A stanza or group of three lines.
terms.long: A tercet may rhyme on all three lines (a triplet), or link to its neighbours as in terza rima (aba bcb), or follow the aba pattern of the villanelle. Dryden and Pope sometimes broke their couplets with a triplet, marked in the margin by a brace. Three-line stanzas feel less settled than couplets or quatrains: a rhyme left over in one tercet can call to the next, which is how terza rima builds its chain. Single rhymed triplets (aaa) give a sense of emphasis or completion, and Herrick and Tennyson wrote whole poems in them.

lines: Come hither, Child! and rest:
This is the end of day,

terms.short: Linked tercets rhyming aba bcb cdc, so that each stanza's middle rhyme leads into the next.
terms.long: Dante invented terza rima for the Divine Comedy, and its chain of rhymes drives the poem forward through a hundred cantos. English, with fewer rhymes, has found it hard to sustain: Wyatt and Byron tried it, Shelley used it in 'Ode to the West Wind' and 'The Triumph of Life', and some translators of Dante, such as Plumptre, kept it.

terms.short: A line of four metrical feet.
terms.long: Iambic tetrameter (eight syllables) is the line of Marvell's 'To His Coy Mistress', Milton's L'Allegro, Scott's verse romances and much of In Memoriam; it is quicker and lighter than pentameter. Trochaic tetrameter is Hiawatha's line; anapaestic tetrameter Byron's Sennacherib's. The ballad stanza alternates four-beat and three-beat lines. Four-beat lines are close to the rhythm of song and of much spoken English, and many traditional and popular verses fall naturally into them. In longer poems iambic tetrameter can feel quick and conversational; poets such as Swift and Samuel Butler used it for comic verse, and Scott for galloping romance.

terms.short: A line of three metrical feet.
terms.long: Short three-beat lines appear in the ballad stanza and common metre (alternating with four-beat lines), in songs and in poems such as Skelton's tumbling 'Skeltonics'. Whole poems in trimeter feel brisk or breathless. A trimeter line holds only a short phrase, so whole poems in it feel quick, light or clipped. Roethke's 'My Papa's Waltz' and many songs are in trimeter. Most often, though, readers meet it as the shorter answering line of a ballad stanza or a hymn, where it brings each half of the stanza to rest.

terms.short: A metrical foot of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one: DUM-de.
terms.long: Trochaic metre has a falling, emphatic, chant-like movement. It is common in songs, charms and children's verse, and in English often drops its last unstressed syllable to end strongly ('TY-ger TY-ger BURN-ing BRIGHT'). Longfellow's Hiawatha is a sustained experiment in trochaic tetrameter, imitating the Finnish Kalevala. A trochee also often begins an iambic line for emphasis. English words of two syllables are very often trochees (garden, water, river), but English phrases tend to begin with light words such as 'the' and 'a', which pull verse towards the iamb. That is one reason sustained trochaic poems are rarer, and why many trochaic lines drop their final weak syllable.

terms.short: The lament 'where are they now?', asking after the vanished great or beloved.
terms.long: From the Latin 'Ubi sunt qui ante nos fuerunt?', 'Where are those who were before us?'. The motif is ancient and widespread: the Old English Wanderer asks where the horse and the rider have gone; Villon asks where are the snows of yesteryear. Its rhetorical questions have no answer, which is their point. The ubi sunt passage is common in medieval Latin sermons and in vernacular poems of many languages, and it often leads to the moral that worldly glory passes and only heavenly things last. Its sequence of questions builds a sense of loss that the poem then answers or leaves open.

terms.short: A play written mainly in verse.
terms.long: Greek tragedy and comedy were in verse, and so was most serious European drama until the nineteenth century. Elizabethan and Jacobean playwrights (Marlowe, Shakespeare, Jonson, Webster) wrote in blank verse, shifting to prose for comic or low characters and to rhyme for songs and scene endings. Later poets wrote verse plays for reading as much as for the stage: Milton's Samson Agonistes, Shelley's Prometheus Unbound, Byron's Manfred.

terms.short: A nineteen-line poem on two rhymes, with two refrains that alternate and meet in the final quatrain.
terms.long: The fixed form of the villanelle was settled in nineteenth-century France, after a sixteenth-century poem by Jean Passerat, and came into English with the vogue for French forms in the 1870s. It has five tercets and a quatrain, all on two rhymes (aba ... abaa). The first line returns as the last line of the second and fourth tercets, the third line as the last line of the third and fifth, and both close the poem as a couplet. The repetitions suit obsession, grief and incantation.

terms.short: The turn in a sonnet's thought, usually at line nine or at the closing couplet.
terms.long: Italian for 'turn'. In the Petrarchan sonnet the volta falls between the octave and the sestet, where the poem shifts from problem to answer, from description to reflection, or from one mood to another; words such as 'but', 'yet' and 'then' often mark it. In the Shakespearean sonnet the turn may come at line nine, or be held back to the final couplet. A strong volta is one of the pleasures of the form: the reader feels the poem change direction. The word is also used, more loosely, of any decisive turn in a short poem.

terms.short: One word governing two others in different senses: 'stain her honour, or her new brocade'.
terms.long: In zeugma (or syllepsis, as some critics prefer for this kind) a single verb or adjective is yoked to two words in different ways, often one literal and one figurative. Pope uses it in The Rape of the Lock to show a world where honour and a dress, a lapdog and a husband, weigh the same. The device depends on the reader noticing a slight shift in meaning between the two uses of the word, and so it often produces a comic jolt. Dickens and Pope both used it; in serious writing it can suggest the uneasy closeness of two things that ought to be kept apart.
